metadata.title: Closures of conjugacy classes in classical real linear Lie groups. II

extraction_notes.note: Mathpix conversion: no theorem environments, labels or section commands (only the References heading), so every node is prose and every section field is empty; the paper's sections 0-17 survive only as enumerate items or 'N. Title.' run-in text.

The formulas (8.9)-(8.17) listing the primitive (2Lambda,Pi)-mutations were lost in conversion (only the tags remain), so they have no equation nodes; the string diagram, the Hasse diagram of Example 2 and the chromosome diagrams of Section 14 exist only as images.

Displays numbered with \tag in starred environments are not reported as facts by latex_facts; I emitted each printed equation number as an equation node by hand (one per numbered row with its own left-hand side), confidence 0.85.

With no headings in the source, the sufficiency proof of Theorem 5 (Sections 9-12) and the proof of Theorem 6 (Sections 15-17) are each one proof node; each section is a top-level step, Lemmas 7-8 and their proofs sit inside the Section 11 step.

nodes.name: Nilpotent orbit
nodes.statement: (An orbit of $G$ in $L$ is nilpotent if it consists of nilpotent elements.)

nodes.name: Vector space V over F
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a (right) F-vector space where $\mathbf{F}=\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{C}$, or $\mathbf{H}$ and let $\operatorname{dim}_{\mathbf{F}} V=n<\infty$.

nodes.name: Real quaternions H
nodes.statement: (By H we denote the division algebra of real quaternions.)

nodes.name: Signature of a hermitian form
nodes.statement: If $f$ : $V \times V \rightarrow \mathbf{F}$ is a nondegenerate hermitian form (including the case of symmetric forms if $\mathbf{F}=\mathbf{R}$ ) then we define the signature of $f$ to be the ordered pair $\operatorname{sig}(f)=\left(n_{+}, n_{-}\right)$where $n_{+}$(resp. $n_{-}$) is the maximum dimension (over $\mathbf{F}$ ) of a positive (resp. negative) definite subspace of $V$. Thus $n_{+}+n_{-}=n$.
nodes.statement_short: sig(f) = (n+, n-), the maximal dimensions of positive and negative definite subspaces of a nondegenerate hermitian form.

nodes.name: Signature of a skew-hermitian form
nodes.statement: When $f$ is a nondegenerate skew-hermitian form (including the case of skew-symmetric forms if $\mathbf{F}=\mathbf{R}$ ) then we set $\operatorname{sig}(f)=(n / 2, n / 2)$.

nodes.name: Classical group (ten series)
nodes.statement: The words classical group will have a technical meaning which we now define. There are ten infinite series of classical groups and we use index $j(1 \leqslant j \leqslant 10)$ to refer to them. The first three series are the general linear groups $$ G L(V) \cong G L_{n}(\mathbf{F}) $$ where $\mathbf{F}=\mathbf{C}$ for $j=1, \mathbf{F}=\mathbf{R}$ for $j=2$, and $\mathbf{F}=\mathbf{H}$ for $j=3$.\\ For the remaining seven series $V$ is equipped with a nondegenerate form $f$ : $V \times V \rightarrow \mathbf{F}$ and the corresponding classical group $G$ is the subgroup of $G L(V)$ which preserves $f$. The type of the form $f$ is specified in Table I for each of these series. \begin{table}[h] \begin{center} \begin{tabular}[t]{|l|l|l|l|l|} \hline $j$ & F & $G$ & $f$ & $\operatorname{sig}(f)$ \\ \hline 4 & C & $U(k, n-k)$ & hermitian & ( $k, n-k$ ) \\ \hline 5 & C & $O_{n}(\mathbf{C})$ & symmetric & \\ \hline 6 & R & $O(k, n-k)$ & symmetric & ( $k, n-k$ ) \\ \hline 7 & H & $O^{*}(2 n)$ & skew-hermitian & ( $n / 2, n / 2$ ) \\ \hline 8 & C & $S p_{2 n}(\mathbf{C})$ & skew-symmetric & \\ \hline 9 & R & $S p_{2 n}(\mathbf{R})$ & skew-symmetric & ( $n, n$ ) \\ \hline 10 & H & $S p(k, n-k)$ & hermitian & ( $k, n-k$ ) \\ \hline \end{tabular} \captionsetup{labelformat=empty} \caption{Table I} \end{center} \end{table}
nodes.statement_short: The ten series j=1..10 of classical groups: GL_n over C, R, H, and the groups preserving the nondegenerate forms of Table I.

nodes.name: SL, SO, SU are not classical
nodes.statement: Note that, according to our definition, the groups $S L_{n}(\mathbf{C}), S L_{n}(\mathbf{R}), S O_{n}(\mathbf{C})$, $S O(k, n-k), S U(k, n-k), S L_{n}(\mathbf{H})$ are not classical.

nodes.name: G, L and the adjoint representation
nodes.statement: From now on $G$ will denote a classical group belonging to the $j$ th series, $L$ its Lie algebra, and $\operatorname{Ad}: G \rightarrow \operatorname{Aut}(L)$ the adjoint representation of $G$.

nodes.name: Notation a.x for the adjoint action
nodes.statement: For $a \in G$ and $x \in L$ we shall write $a \cdot x$ instead of $\operatorname{Ad}(a)(x)$.

nodes.name: G-orbit G.x
nodes.statement: Thus $G \cdot x=\{a \cdot x: a \in G\}$ is the $G$-orbit in $L$ containing $x$.

nodes.name: Centralizer C_G(x)
nodes.statement: The centralizer $C_{G}(x)$ of $x \in L$ in $G$ is the subgroup of $G$ consisting of all elements $a$ such that $a \cdot x=x$.
differentia: consisting of all elements $a$ such that $a \cdot x=x$

nodes.name: Lie algebra L of a classical group
nodes.statement: If $1 \leqslant j \leqslant 3$ we identify $L$ with the Lie algebra of all $\mathbf{F}$-linear transformations of $V$. If $4 \leqslant j \leqslant 10$ then we identify $L$ with the Lie algebra of all $\mathbf{F}$-linear transformations $x$ of $V$ which satisfy $f\left(x\left(v_{1}\right), v_{2}\right)+f\left(v_{1}, x\left(v_{2}\right)\right)=0$ for all $v_{1}, v_{2} \in V$.

nodes.name: Generalized eigenspace V(zeta, x)
nodes.statement: Let $x \in L$ be arbitrary. If $\mathbf{F}=\mathbf{C}$ we define for $\zeta \in \mathbf{C}$ the subspace $V(\zeta, x)$ of $V$ to be $$ V(\zeta, x)=\operatorname{Ker}(x-\zeta)^{\infty}, $$ i.e., it is the kernel of $(x-\zeta)^{k}$ for large $k$, say $k=n$. If $\mathbf{F}=\mathbf{R}$ of $\mathbf{H}$ we define for $\zeta \in \mathbf{C}$ the subspace $V(\zeta, x)$ of $V$ by $$ V(\zeta, x)=\operatorname{Ker}\left(x^{2}-2 \operatorname{Re}(\zeta) x+|\zeta|^{2}\right)^{\infty} . $$

nodes.name: Eigenvalue of x
nodes.statement: We say that $\zeta \in \mathbf{C}$ is an eigenvalue of $x \in L$ if $V(\zeta, x) \neq 0$.

nodes.name: Orthogonality of generalized eigenspaces
nodes.statement: It is well known that for $j \in\{5,6\}$ we have $V(\zeta, x) \perp V\left(\zeta^{\prime}, x\right)$ if $\zeta+\zeta^{\prime} \neq 0$, and for $j \in\{4,6,7,9,10\}$ we have $V(\zeta, x) \perp V\left(\zeta^{\prime}, x\right)$ if $\bar{\zeta}+\zeta^{\prime} \neq 0$. (The orthogonality is with respect to the form $f$.)
conclusions: $V(\zeta, x) \perp V\left(\zeta^{\prime}, x\right)$ if $\zeta+\zeta^{\prime} \neq 0$
$V(\zeta, x) \perp V\left(\zeta^{\prime}, x\right)$ if $\bar{\zeta}+\zeta^{\prime} \neq 0$

nodes.name: Subspace V'(zeta, x)
nodes.statement: This suggests that we introduce the following definition: $$ V^{\prime}(\zeta, x)= \begin{cases}V(\zeta, x) & \text { for } j \in\{1,2,3\} \\ V(\zeta, x)+V(-\zeta, x) & \text { for } j \in\{5,8\} \\ V(\zeta, x)+v(-\bar{\zeta}, x) & \text { for } j \in\{4,6,7,9,10\}\end{cases} $$

nodes.name: Decomposition of V into V'(zeta, x)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} V=\sum_{\zeta \in \Omega_{j}} V^{\prime}(\zeta, x) . \tag{2.1} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Index set Omega_j
nodes.statement: The set $\Omega_{j}$ is the subset of $\mathbf{C}$ specified by the conditions stated in Table II. \begin{table}[h] \begin{center} \begin{tabular}[t]{|l|l|l|l|} \hline $j$ & & $\Omega_{j}$ & \\ \hline 1 & C & & \\ \hline 2, 3 & $\operatorname{Im} \zeta \geqslant 0$ & & \\ \hline 4 & $\operatorname{Re} \zeta \geqslant 0$ & & \\ \hline 5,8 & $\operatorname{Im} \zeta>0$ & or & $\zeta \geqslant 0$ \\ \hline 6, 7, 9, 10 & $\operatorname{Re} \zeta \geqslant 0$ & and & $\operatorname{Im} \zeta \geqslant 0$ \\ \hline \end{tabular} \captionsetup{labelformat=empty} \caption{Table II} \end{center} \end{table}

nodes.name: Restrictions x_zeta and x'_zeta
nodes.statement: For $\zeta \in \mathbf{C}$ let $x_{\zeta}$ (resp. $x_{\zeta}^{\prime}$ ) be the restriction of $x$ to $V(\zeta, x)$ (resp. $V^{\prime}(\zeta, x)$ ).

nodes.name: Classical group G(zeta, x)
nodes.statement: If $1 \leqslant j \leqslant 3$ let $G(\zeta, x)$ be the general linear group of the space $V(\zeta, x)$. If $4 \leqslant j \leqslant 10$ let $G(\zeta, x)$ be the group of all $\mathbf{F}$-linear automorphisms of $V^{\prime}(\zeta, x)$ which preserve the restriction of the form $f$ to $V^{\prime}(\zeta, x)$. (This restriction is clearly nondegenerate.) Thus in all cases $G(\zeta, x)$ is a classical group of the $j$ th series.

nodes.name: Lie algebra L(zeta, x)
nodes.statement: If $L(\zeta, x)$ is the Lie algebra of $G(\zeta, x)$ then $x_{\zeta}^{\prime} \in L(\zeta, x)$.

nodes.name: Centralizer C(zeta, x)
nodes.statement: Finally let $C(\zeta, x)$ be the centralizer of $x_{\zeta}^{\prime}$ in $G(\zeta, x)$.

nodes.name: Centralizer as product of C(zeta, x)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} C_{G}(x)=\prod_{\zeta \in \Omega_{j}} C(\zeta, x) . \tag{2.2} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Centralizer Theorem
nodes.statement: Theorem 1. Let $G$ be a classical group of the jth series, $L$ its Lie algebra, and $x \in L$ a semisimple element. Then each $C(\zeta, x)$ in (2.2) is a classical group of $k$ th series where $k$ depends only on $j$ and $\zeta$.
assumptions: Let $G$ be a classical group of the jth series, $L$ its Lie algebra, and $x \in L$ a semisimple element.
conclusions: each $C(\zeta, x)$ in (2.2) is a classical group of $k$ th series where $k$ depends only on $j$ and $\zeta$
also_stated_at: In §2 we state the Centralizer Theorem (Theorem 1) which asserts that the centralizer $C_{G}(x)$ in $G$ of a semisimple element $x \in L$ is a direct product of classical groups.
nodes.statement_short: For semisimple x, each factor C(zeta,x) of the centralizer is a classical group whose series k depends only on j and zeta.

nodes.name: Series of the centralizer factors (Table III)
Jordan decomposition
nodes.statement: Every $x \in L$ has a unique Jordan decomposition $x=x_{s}+x_{n}$, where $x_{s} \in L$ is semisimple, $x_{n} \in L$ is nilpotent, and $\left[x_{s}, x_{n}\right]=0$.
also_stated_at: Let $x \in L$ and let $x=x_{s}+x_{n}$ be its Jordan decomposition. (This means that $x_{s}, x_{n} \in L, x_{s}$ is semisimple, $x_{n}$ is nilpotent, and $\left[x_{s}, x_{n}\right]=0$.)

nodes.name: Semisimple and nilpotent components
nodes.statement: We refer to $x_{s}$ (resp. $x_{n}$ ) as the semisimple (resp. nilpotent) component of $x$.

nodes.name: Reduction theorem for orbit closures
nodes.statement: Theorem 2. Let $G$ be a classical group, $L$ its Lie algebra, $x$ and $y$ elements of $L$, and $x=x_{s}+x_{n}$ the Jordan decomposition of $x$. Then $y \in \overline{G \cdot x}$ iff $a \cdot y=x_{s}+z$ for some $a \in G$ and some \begin{equation*} z \in \overline{C_{G}\left(x_{s}\right) \cdot x_{n}} . \tag{3.1} \end{equation*}
assumptions: Let $G$ be a classical group, $L$ its Lie algebra, $x$ and $y$ elements of $L$, and $x=x_{s}+x_{n}$ the Jordan decomposition of $x$.
conclusions: Then $y \in \overline{G \cdot x}$ iff $a \cdot y=x_{s}+z$ for some $a \in G$ and some
equivalent_conditions: $a \cdot y=x_{s}+z$ for some $a \in G$ and some
also_stated_at: Theorem 2 asserts that if $y$ belongs to the closure of the orbit $G \cdot x$ then there exists an element $z$ in the closure of the orbit $C_{G}\left(x_{s}\right) \cdot x_{n}$ such that $x_{s}+z \in G \cdot y$.
nodes.statement_short: y lies in the closure of G.x iff some conjugate of y is x_s + z with z in the closure of the C_G(x_s)-orbit of x_n.

nodes.name: Closure condition on z
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} z \in \overline{C_{G}\left(x_{s}\right) \cdot x_{n}} . \tag{3.1} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Argument for the reduction to the nilpotent case
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{O}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{O}_{2}$ be $G$-orbits in $L$. Assume that $\mathcal{O}_{1} \subset \overline{\mathcal{O}}_{2}$, which we shall also write as $\mathcal{O}_{1} \leqslant \mathcal{O}_{2}$. By Theorem 2 we can choose $x \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ and $y \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$ such that $y=x_{s}+z$ and $z$ satisfies (3.1). Clearly, $z$ is the nilpotent part of $y, z=y_{n}$. By Theorem 1 we have \begin{equation*} C_{G}\left(x_{s}\right)=C\left(\zeta_{1}, x_{s}\right) \times \cdots \times C\left(\zeta_{m}, x_{s}\right) \tag{3.2} \end{equation*} where $\zeta_{1}, \ldots, \zeta_{m}$ are the distinct eigenvalues of $x_{s}$ belonging to $\Omega_{j}$.\\ Let $Z_{I}\left(x_{s}\right)$ be the centralizer of $x_{s}$ in $L$, i.e., $Z_{L}\left(x_{s}\right)=\left\{t \in L:\left[t, x_{s}\right]=0\right\}$.\\ We denote by $L\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$ the Lie algebra of $G\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$, and let $Z\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$ be the centralizer in $L\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$ of the restriction of $x_{s}$ to $V^{\prime}\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$. It is clear that $Z_{L}\left(x_{s}\right)$ is the Lie algebra of $C_{G}\left(x_{s}\right)$, and $Z\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$ is the Lie algebra of $C\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$. It follows from (3.2) that \begin{equation*} Z_{L}\left(x_{s}\right)=Z\left(\zeta_{1}, x_{s}\right) \oplus \cdots \oplus Z\left(\zeta_{m}, x_{s}\right) . \tag{3.3} \end{equation*} Since $x_{n}, z \in Z_{L}\left(x_{s}\right)$, we have $$ x_{n}=x_{n}^{(1)}+\cdots+x_{n}^{(m)}, \quad z=z^{(1)}+\cdots+z^{(m)}, $$ where $x_{n}^{(k)}, z^{(k)} \in Z\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$ for $1 \leqslant k \leqslant m$.\\ It follows from (3.1) to (3.3) that $z^{(k)} \in \overline{C\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right) \cdot x_{n}^{(k)}}, 1 \leqslant k \leqslant m$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 2, then split C_G(x_s) and its Lie algebra into the factors of Theorem 1 and project componentwise.

nodes.name: Factorization of C_G(x_s)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} C_{G}\left(x_{s}\right)=C\left(\zeta_{1}, x_{s}\right) \times \cdots \times C\left(\zeta_{m}, x_{s}\right) \tag{3.2} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Decomposition of Z_L(x_s)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} Z_{L}\left(x_{s}\right)=Z\left(\zeta_{1}, x_{s}\right) \oplus \cdots \oplus Z\left(\zeta_{m}, x_{s}\right) . \tag{3.3} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Reduction to the nilpotent case
nodes.statement: Thus the $G$-orbits in $L$ which are contained in the closure of the orbit $G \cdot x$ can be easily found provided we know which orbits of $C\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$ in $Z\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$ are contained in the closure of the orbit $C\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right) \cdot x_{n}^{(k)}, 1 \leqslant k \leqslant n$.
conclusions: Thus the $G$-orbits in $L$ which are contained in the closure of the orbit $G \cdot x$ can be easily found provided we know which orbits of $C\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$ in $Z\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$ are contained in the closure of the orbit $C\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right) \cdot x_{n}^{(k)}, 1 \leqslant k \leqslant n$.
nodes.statement_short: Orbits in the closure of G.x are determined by nilpotent orbit closures in the classical factors C(zeta_k, x_s).

nodes.name: All series must be treated simultaneously
nodes.statement: Since $C\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$ is a classical group and $x_{n}^{(k)} \in Z\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$ is nilpotent, we have indeed reduced the general problem to the nilpotent case. Note that (by assumption) $G$ belongs to the $j$ th series but the groups $C\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$ may belong to some other series of classical groups. This is the reason why we have to consider simultaneously all classical groups.

nodes.name: Order on orbits
nodes.statement: Recall that for two $G$-orbits $\mathcal{O}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{O}_{2}$ in $L$ we write $\mathcal{O}_{1} \leqslant \mathcal{O}_{2}$ if $\mathcal{O}_{1} \subset \overline{\mathcal{O}}_{2}$.

nodes.name: Gerstenhaber's theorem on nilpotent orbit closures (rank criterion)
nodes.statement: Theorem 3. Let $G$ be a classical group of jth series with $j \in\{1,2,3,5,8\}$, and $L$ its Lie algebra. If $x, y \in L$ are nilpotent then $G \cdot x \leqslant G \cdot y$ holds iff $\operatorname{rank}\left(x^{k}\right) \leqslant \operatorname{rank}\left(y^{k}\right)$ for all $k(\geqslant 0)$.
assumptions: Let $G$ be a classical group of jth series with $j \in\{1,2,3,5,8\}$, and $L$ its Lie algebra.
conclusions: $G \cdot x \leqslant G \cdot y$ holds iff $\operatorname{rank}\left(x^{k}\right) \leqslant \operatorname{rank}\left(y^{k}\right)$ for all $k(\geqslant 0)$

nodes.name: Standing assumption j in {4,6,7,9,10}
nodes.statement: From now on we shall assume that $j \in\{4,6,7,9,10\}$.
also_stated_at: Recall that we assume that $G$ is a classical group of the $j$ th series with $j \in\{4,6,7,9,10\}$.

nodes.name: Type (equivalence class of triples)
nodes.statement: For a fixed $j$ we consider the triples ( $V, f, x$ ) where $V$ and $f$ are specified by Table I and $x \in L$, where $L$ is the Lie algebra of the corresponding classical group $G$. An equivalence class of such triples is called a type; see [1] for precise definition.

nodes.name: Sum of types
nodes.statement: Let $\Delta$ be the type containing the triple $(V, f, x)$. There exists a direct decomposition $V=V_{1} \oplus \cdots \oplus V_{r}$ into $x$-invariant nonzero nondegenerate subspaces which are orthogonal to each other and moreover the summands $V_{1}, \ldots, V_{r}$ cannot be further decomposed in the same sense. Let $x_{k}$ and $f_{k}$ be the restrictions of $x$ and $f$, respectively, to $V_{k}$. If $\Delta_{k}$ is the type containing ( $V_{k}, f_{k}, x_{k}$ ) then we shall write $\Delta=\Delta_{1}+\cdots+\Delta_{r}$.

nodes.name: Indecomposable type
nodes.statement: We say that $\Delta$ is indecomposable if $\Delta \neq 0$ (i.e., $\operatorname{dim} V \neq 0$ ) and $\Delta$ cannot be written as a sum of two nonzero types.

nodes.name: Unique decomposition into indecomposable types
nodes.statement: In general, $\Delta$ can be\\[0pt] expressed as a sum of indecomposable types and as shown in [1] such a decomposition is unique.
conclusions: $\Delta$ can be\\[0pt] expressed as a sum of indecomposable types
such a decomposition is unique

nodes.name: Nilpotent type
nodes.statement: If $x$ is nilpotent we say that the type $\Delta$ is also nilpotent.

nodes.name: Classification of nilpotent indecomposable types (Table IV)
nodes.statement: The nilpotent indecomposable types are listed in the second column of Table IV. (At present ignore the last two columns of this table.) \begin{table}[h] \begin{center} \begin{tabular}[t]{|l|l|l|l|} \hline $j$ & $\Delta$ & $X$ & $\Phi_{j}$ \\ \hline 4 & $\Delta_{m}^{\varepsilon}(0)$ & $g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)$ & $\Pi$ \\ \hline 6 & \( \begin{gathered} \Delta_{m}^{\varepsilon}(0), m \text { even } \\ \Delta_{m}(0,0), m \text { odd } \end{gathered} \) & \( \begin{aligned} & g^{\varepsilon}(m+1) \\ & 2 g(m+1) \end{aligned} \) & $(2 \Lambda, \Pi)$ \\ \hline 7 & \( \begin{gathered} \Delta_{m}(0,0), m \text { even } \\ \Delta_{m}^{\varepsilon}(0,0), m \text { odd } \end{gathered} \) & \( \begin{aligned} & g(m+1) \\ & g^{\epsilon}(m+1) \end{aligned} \) & $(\Pi, \Lambda)$ \\ \hline 9 & \( \begin{gathered} \Delta_{m}(0,0), m \text { even } \\ \Delta_{m}^{e}(0), m \text { odd } \end{gathered} \) & \( \begin{gathered} 2 g(m+1) \\ g^{\varepsilon}(m+1) \end{gathered} \) & $(\Pi, 2 \Lambda)$ \\ \hline 10 & \( \begin{aligned} & \Delta_{m}^{\varepsilon}(0,0), m \text { even } \\ & \Delta_{m}(0,0), m \text { odd } \end{aligned} \) & \( \begin{aligned} & g^{\varepsilon}(m+1) \\ & g(m+1) \end{aligned} \) & ( $\Lambda, \Pi$ ) \\ \hline \end{tabular} \captionsetup{labelformat=empty} \caption{Table IV} \end{center} \end{table} In this table $\varepsilon= \pm$ and $m(\geqslant 0)$ is an integer.
nodes.statement_short: Table IV lists the nilpotent indecomposable types for j=4,6,7,9,10 with their chromosomes X and varieties Phi_j.

nodes.name: Representatives of the polarized nilpotent types
nodes.statement: We shall now describe representative triples $(V, f, x)$ for each of the types in this table. We warn the reader that our designation of types $\Delta_{m}^{+}$and $\Delta_{m}^{-}$differs from that adopted in [1]. If $j=4$ a representative of $\Delta_{m}^{\varepsilon}(0)$ is given by:\\ $V$ a complex vector space,\\ $e_{0}, e_{1}, \ldots, e_{m}$ a basis of $V$, \begin{equation*} x\left(e_{k}\right)=e_{k+1} i \quad(i=\sqrt{-1}, 0 \leqslant k<m), \quad x\left(e_{m}\right)=0, \tag{5.1} \end{equation*} $f$ a hermitian form on $V$,\\ $f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}\right)=\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m}\left(\delta_{i j}\right.$ Kronecker symbol $)$.\\ If $j=6$, a representative of $\Delta_{m}^{\varepsilon}(0), m$ even, say $m=2 m^{\prime}$, is given by:\\ $V$ a real vector space,\\ $e_{0}, e_{1}, \ldots, e_{m}$ a basis of $V$, \begin{align*} & x\left(e_{k}\right)=e_{k+1} \quad\left(0 \leqslant k<m^{\prime}\right), \\ & x\left(e_{k}\right)=-e_{k+1} \quad\left(m^{\prime} \leqslant k<m\right), x\left(e_{m}\right)=0, \tag{5.2} \end{align*} $f$ a symmetric bilinear form on $V$,\\ $f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}\right)=\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m}$.\\ If $j=7$ a representative of $\Delta_{m}^{\varepsilon}(0,0), m$ odd, is given by:\\ $V$ a (right) quaternionic vector space,\\ $e_{0}, e_{1}, \ldots, e_{m}$ a basis of $V$,\\ $x$ given by (5.1),\\ $f$ a skew-hermitian form on $V$,\\ $f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}\right)=-i \varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m}$. If $j=9$ a representative of $\Delta_{m}^{\varepsilon}(0), m$ odd, say $m=2 m^{\prime}-1$, is given by:\\ $V$ a real vector space,\\ $e_{0}, e_{1}, \ldots, e_{m}$ a basis of $V$,\\ $x$ given by (5.2),\\ $f$ a skew-symmetric form on $V$,\\ $f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}\right)=\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m}$ for $r<s$.\\ If $j=10$ then a representative of $\Delta_{m}^{\varepsilon}(0,0), m$ even, is given by:\\ $V$ a (right) quaternionic vector space,\\ $e_{0}, e_{1}, \ldots, e_{m}$ a basis of $V$,\\ $x$ given by (5.1),\\ $f$ a hermitian form on $V$,\\ $f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}\right)=\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m}$.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit basis models (V, f, x) of the polarized indecomposable nilpotent types for j=4,6,7,9,10, fixing the paper's sign convention.

nodes.name: Model nilpotent x on a basis
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} x\left(e_{k}\right)=e_{k+1} i \quad(i=\sqrt{-1}, 0 \leqslant k<m), \quad x\left(e_{m}\right)=0, \tag{5.1} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Model nilpotent x for j=6,9
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} & x\left(e_{k}\right)=e_{k+1} \quad\left(0 \leqslant k<m^{\prime}\right), \\ & x\left(e_{k}\right)=-e_{k+1} \quad\left(m^{\prime} \leqslant k<m\right), x\left(e_{m}\right)=0, \tag{5.2} \end{align*}

nodes.name: Sign inequalities distinguishing Delta^+ and Delta^-
nodes.statement: The nilpotent types $\Delta_{m}^{+}$and $\Delta_{m}^{-}$can be distinguished by a simple inequality. Indeed, if $(V, f, x)$ is one of the representatives listed above then for all $v \in V$ we have \begin{align*} (-i)^{m} \varepsilon f\left(v, x^{m}(v)\right) \geqslant 0 . & \text { if } j=4, \tag{5.3}\\ i^{m} \varepsilon f\left(v, x^{m}(v)\right) \geqslant 0 & \text { if } j=6,10, \tag{5.4}\\ i^{m-1} \varepsilon f\left(v, x^{m}(v)\right) \geqslant 0 & \text { if } j=7,9 . \tag{5.5} \end{align*}
assumptions: if $(V, f, x)$ is one of the representatives listed above
conclusions: for all $v \in V$ we have
nodes.statement_short: On the representatives, (-i)^m eps f(v, x^m v) >= 0 (j=4) and analogous sign conditions (j=6,7,9,10) determine eps.

nodes.name: Sign inequality for j=4
nodes.statement: (-i)^{m} \varepsilon f\left(v, x^{m}(v)\right) \geqslant 0 . & \text { if } j=4, \tag{5.3}

nodes.name: Sign inequality for j=6,10
nodes.statement: i^{m} \varepsilon f\left(v, x^{m}(v)\right) \geqslant 0 & \text { if } j=6,10, \tag{5.4}

nodes.name: Sign inequality for j=7,9
nodes.statement: i^{m-1} \varepsilon f\left(v, x^{m}(v)\right) \geqslant 0 & \text { if } j=7,9 . \tag{5.5}

nodes.name: Representatives of the nonpolarized nilpotent types
nodes.statement: If $j=6$ (resp. 9) a representative of $\Delta_{m}(0,0), m$ odd (resp. even) is given by:\\ $V$ a real vector space,\\ $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{m}, e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{m}^{\prime}$ a basis of $V$, $$ \begin{array}{lll} x\left(e_{k}\right)=e_{k+1} & (0 \leqslant k<m), & x\left(e_{m}\right)=0, \\ x\left(e_{k}^{\prime}\right)=-e_{k+1}^{\prime} & (0 \leqslant k<m), & x\left(e_{m}^{\prime}\right)=0, \end{array} $$ $f$ is a symmetric (resp. skew-symmetric) form on $V$, $$ f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}\right)=f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}\right)=0, f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}\right)=\delta_{r+s, m} . $$ If $j=7$ then a representative of $\Delta_{m}(0,0)$ with $m$ even has the same description as the representative of $\Delta_{m}^{\varepsilon}(0,0)$ with $m$ odd. (The choice of $\varepsilon= \pm$ is not important since both represent the same type.) Similarly, if $j=10$ then a representative of $\Delta_{m}(0,0)$ with $m$ odd has the same description as the representative of $\Delta_{m}^{\varepsilon}(0,0)$ with $m$ even.
nodes.statement_short: Basis models of the nonpolarized types Delta_m(0,0) for j=6,9 (two Jordan chains paired by f) and their identification for j=7,10.

nodes.name: String
nodes.statement: A string (nonpolarized) $S$ is a directed graph isomorphic to\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{3049372b-fe1b-4647-987b-29640168b2a6-09_75_722_2057_409} The vertex 1 is the head and the vertex $n$ the tail of this string; $n$ is its rank.

nodes.name: Polarized string
nodes.statement: If we assign alternating + and - signs to the vertices of this string we obtain a polarized string.

nodes.name: Positive and negative polarized strings
nodes.statement: A polarized string is positive or negative depending on whether its tail carries a + or - sign.

nodes.name: Signature of a string
nodes.statement: The signature of a polarized string $S$ is the ordered pair \begin{equation*} \operatorname{sig} S=\left(r^{+}, r^{-}\right) \tag{6.1} \end{equation*} where $r^{+}$and $r^{-}$are the numbers of vertices of $S$ with label + and - , respectively. If $S$ is nonpolarized we define its signature by (6.1) where now $r^{+}=r^{-}=\frac{1}{2} n, n$ being the rank of $S$.

nodes.name: Signature of a string
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} \operatorname{sig} S=\left(r^{+}, r^{-}\right) \tag{6.1} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Gene
nodes.statement: A gene is an isomorphism class of strings; it may be polarized or nonpolarized.

nodes.name: Genes g(n), g+(n), g-(n)
nodes.statement: There are precisely three genes of rank $n$ for each positive integer $n$ : the nonpolarized gene of rank $n$, the positive gene of rank $n$, and the negative gene of rank $n$. We shall denote these three genes in that order by $g(n), g^{+}(n)$, and $g^{-}(n)$.

nodes.name: Free abelian group Sigma on genes
nodes.statement: Let $\Sigma$ be the free abelian group having the set of genes as its basis; the elements of $\Sigma$ will be written as formal finite integral linear combinations of genes.

nodes.name: Chromosome
nodes.statement: A chromosome is an element of $\Sigma$ which is a nonnegative integral linear combination of genes.
differentia: nonnegative integral linear combination of genes

nodes.name: Monoid of chromosomes Sigma+
nodes.statement: The set of all chromosomes will be denoted by $\Sigma^{+}$; it is clearly a free commutative monoid on the set of genes.

nodes.name: Containment of chromosomes
nodes.statement: If $X=Y+Z$ where $Y$ and $Z$ are chromosomes then we say that $X$ contains $Y$, and we write $X \supset Y$ or $Y \subset X$.

nodes.name: Multiplicity of a gene
nodes.statement: If $g$ is a gene and $m(\geqslant 0)$ integer such that $X \supset m g$ and $X \not \supset(m+1) g$ then we say that $m$ is the multiplicity of $g$ in the chromosome $X$.

nodes.name: Gene occurring in a chromosome
nodes.statement: We say that $g$ occurs in $X$ if its multiplicity $m$ in $X$ is not zero.

nodes.name: Signature and rank of a chromosome
nodes.statement: The signature of a chromosome $X$ is by definition the sum of the signatures of its genes (taking into account the multiplicities). Similarly, one defines the rank of $X$.

nodes.name: Even, odd, polarized and nonpolarized chromosomes
nodes.statement: A chromosome is called even (resp. odd, polarized, nonpolarized) if all its constituent genes have even rank (resp. have odd rank, are polarized, are non-polarized).

nodes.name: Even and odd parts e(X), o(X)
nodes.statement: Every chromosome $X$ admits a unique decomposition $X=e(X)+o(X)$ where $e(X)$ is an even and $o(X)$ an odd chromosome.

nodes.name: Variety of chromosomes
nodes.statement: A variety is a submonoid of $\Sigma^{+}$.

nodes.name: Varieties Pi and Lambda
nodes.statement: By $\Pi$ (resp. $\Lambda$ ) we denote the variety of polarized (resp. nonpolarized) chromosomes.

nodes.name: Variety k Phi
nodes.statement: If $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$ is a variety, so is $k \boldsymbol{\Phi}=\{k X$ : $X \in \Phi\}$, for every nonnegative integer $k$.

nodes.name: Rank-n part Phi(n)
nodes.statement: If $\Phi$ is a variety and $n(\geqslant 0)$ an integer then $\Phi(n)$ denotes the set of all $X \in \Phi$ having rank $n$.

nodes.name: Variety (Phi, Psi)
nodes.statement: If $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ are varieties then $(\Phi, \Psi)$ denotes the variety consisting of all chromosomes $X$ such that $e(X) \in \Phi$ and $o(X) \in \Psi$.

nodes.name: The five varieties
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} \Pi, \quad(\Lambda, \Pi), \quad(\Pi, \Lambda), \quad(2 \Lambda, \Pi), \quad(\Pi, 2 \Lambda) . \tag{6.2} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Priming of a gene g'
nodes.statement: If $g$ is a gene of rank $n(>1)$ we define $g^{\prime}$ as follows $$ \begin{aligned} g^{\prime} & =g(n-1) & & \text { if } g=g(n), \\ & =g^{+}(n-1) & & \text { if } g=g^{+}(n), \\ & =g^{-}(n-1) & & \text { if } g=g^{-}(n) . \end{aligned} $$ If $g$ is a gene of rank 1 we set $g^{\prime}=0$.

nodes.name: Priming of a chromosome X'
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a chromosome then we define $X^{\prime}$ by applying this "prime" operation to each of its constituent genes.

nodes.name: Iterated primes X^(k)
nodes.statement: Now we define inductively the chromosome $X^{(k)}, k \geqslant 0$, as follows: $$ X^{(0)}=X, \quad X^{(k+1)}=\left(X^{(k)}\right)^{\prime} \quad \text { for } k \geqslant 0 . $$

nodes.name: Example of the priming operation
nodes.statement: For instance, if $X=2 g(3)+g^{-}(2)+g(2)+g^{+}$(4) then $$ \begin{gathered} X^{\prime}=X^{(1)}=2 g(2)+g^{-}(1)+g(1)+g^{+}(3), \\ X^{(2)}=2 g(1)+g^{+}(2), \quad X^{(3)}=g^{+}(1), \quad X^{(k)}=0 \quad \text { for } k \geqslant 4 . \end{gathered} $$

nodes.name: Order on ordered pairs
nodes.statement: For ordered pairs of real numbers, the inequality $(p, q) \leqslant(r, s)$ will stand for $p \leqslant r$ and $q \leqslant s$.

nodes.name: Dominance order on chromosomes
nodes.statement: We say that a chromosome $X$ dominates a chromosome $Y$, and we write $X \geqslant Y$ or $Y \leqslant X$, if $$ \operatorname{sig} X^{(k)} \geqslant \operatorname{sig} Y^{(k)}, \quad \forall k . $$
nodes.statement_short: X dominates Y when sig X^(k) >= sig Y^(k) componentwise for every k.

nodes.name: Dominance is a partial order
nodes.statement: It is easy to check that in each of the varieties (6.2) the dominance relation is a partial order.
conclusions: the dominance relation is a partial order

nodes.name: Chromosome X(Delta) of an indecomposable type
nodes.statement: To each indecomposable nilpotent type $\Delta$ of the $j$ th series we associate a chromosome $X=X(\Delta)$ belonging to a variety $\Phi_{j}$. The chromosome $X$ and the variety $\Phi_{j}$ are specified in the last two columns of Table IV.

nodes.name: Chromosome X(Delta) of a nilpotent type
nodes.statement: More generally if $\Delta$ is a nilpotent type of the $j$ th series and $\Delta=\Delta_{1}+\cdots+\Delta_{r}$ is its decomposition into indecomposable types then we define $X(\Delta)=X\left(\Delta_{1}\right)$ $+\cdots+X\left(\Delta_{r}\right)$.

nodes.name: Types correspond bijectively to chromosomes
nodes.statement: Clearly the map $\Delta \mapsto X(\Delta)$ from the set of nilpotent types of the $j$ th series to $\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{j}$ is a bijection.
conclusions: the map $\Delta \mapsto X(\Delta)$ from the set of nilpotent types of the $j$ th series to $\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{j}$ is a bijection

nodes.name: Type Delta(O) of a nilpotent orbit
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{O}$ be a nilpotent $G$-orbit in $L$. If $x, y \in \mathcal{O}$ then the triples $(V, f, x)$ and ( $V, f, y$ ) are equivalent and hence we can associate a type $\Delta=\Delta(\mathcal{O})$ to the orbit $\mathcal{O}$.

nodes.name: Chromosome X(O) of a nilpotent orbit
nodes.statement: We shall write $X(\mathcal{O})$ instead of $X(\Delta(\mathcal{O}))$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement: The following lemma is an immediate consequence of our definitions and the description of nilpotent $G$-orbits in $L$ given in $\S 5$.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definitions and the description of nilpotent orbits in Section 5.

nodes.name: Chromosome parametrization of nilpotent orbits
nodes.statement: Lemma 4. The map $\mathcal{O}_{\mapsto} X(\mathcal{O})$ defined above is a bijection from the set of nilpotent $G$-orbits in $L$ to the set of chromosomes $X \in \Phi_{j}$ satisfying the condition $\operatorname{sig} X=\operatorname{sig}(f)$.
also_stated_at: In §7 we establish (Lemma 4) a bijection between the nilpotent orbits of the classical group $G$ of the $j$ th series defined by ( $V, f$ ) and the set of chromosomes $X$ in $\Phi_{j}$ such that $\operatorname{sig} X=\operatorname{sig}(f)$.
conclusions: The map $\mathcal{O}_{\mapsto} X(\mathcal{O})$ defined above is a bijection from the set of nilpotent $G$-orbits in $L$ to the set of chromosomes $X \in \Phi_{j}$ satisfying the condition $\operatorname{sig} X=\operatorname{sig}(f)$.
nodes.statement_short: Nilpotent G-orbits in L correspond bijectively to chromosomes in Phi_j with signature sig(f).

nodes.name: Nilpotent orbits of Sp(2,2)
nodes.statement: Example 1. Let $j=10$ and $\operatorname{sig}(f)=(2,2)$. Then there are six nilpotent orbits in $L$; their types are $$ \begin{gathered} 2 \Delta_{0}^{+}(0,0)+2 \Delta_{0}^{-}(0,0), \quad \Delta_{0}^{+}(0,0)+\Delta_{0}^{-}(0,0)+\Delta_{1}(0,0), \quad 2 \Delta_{1}(0,0), \\ \Delta_{0}^{+}(0,0)+\Delta_{2}^{-}(0,0), \quad \Delta_{0}^{-}(0,0)+\Delta_{2}^{+}(0,0), \quad \Delta_{3}(0,0) . \end{gathered} $$ These types are also listed in [1, p. 351] but the superscripts ± do not coincide due to the different definition which we have introduced. The chromosomes in $(\Lambda, \Pi)$ corresponding to these types are $2 g^{+}(1)+2 g^{-}(1)$, $g^{+}(1)+g^{-}(1)+g(2), 2 g(2), g^{+}(1)+g^{-}(3), g^{-}(1)+g^{+}(3)$, and $g(4)$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: For j=10, sig(f)=(2,2) there are six nilpotent orbits; their types and chromosomes in (Lambda, Pi) are listed.

nodes.name: Closure ordering of nilpotent orbits via chromosomes
nodes.statement: Theorem 5. If $\mathcal{O}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{O}_{2}$ are nilpotent orbits of $G$ in its Lie algebra $L$ then $\mathcal{O}_{1} \subset \overline{\mathcal{O}}_{2}$ holds iff $X\left(\mathcal{O}_{1}\right) \leqslant X\left(\mathcal{O}_{2}\right)$.
also_stated_at: It says that a nilpotent orbit $\mathcal{O}_{1}$ is contained in the closure of the nilpotent orbit $\mathcal{O}_{2}$ iff their corresponding chromosomes $X\left(\mathcal{O}_{1}\right)$ and $X\left(\mathcal{O}_{2}\right)$ satisfy the inequality $X\left(\mathcal{O}_{1}\right) \leqslant X\left(\mathcal{O}_{2}\right)$.
assumptions: $\mathcal{O}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{O}_{2}$ are nilpotent orbits of $G$ in its Lie algebra $L$
conclusions: $\mathcal{O}_{1} \subset \overline{\mathcal{O}}_{2}$ holds iff $X\left(\mathcal{O}_{1}\right) \leqslant X\left(\mathcal{O}_{2}\right)$
nodes.statement_short: For j in {4,6,7,9,10}, a nilpotent orbit lies in the closure of another iff its chromosome is dominated by the other's.

nodes.name: Necessity part of Theorem 5 is in [4]
nodes.statement: The necessity of the condition $X\left(\mathcal{O}_{1}\right) \leqslant X\left(\mathcal{O}_{2}\right)$ was proved in [4].

nodes.name: Hasse diagram of nilpotent orbits of Sp(2,2)
nodes.statement: Example 2. As we saw in Example 1, the group $S p(2,2)$ has 6 nilpotent orbits in its Lie algebra. The partially ordered set of these orbits (with respect to the ordering $\leqslant$ ) is represented by the diagram\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{3049372b-fe1b-4647-987b-29640168b2a6-12_784_457_499_526}\\ where the orbits are represented by their chromosomes and the rows of dots represent nonpolarized genes. Of course the bottom chromosome $2 g^{+}(1)+2 g^{-}(1)$ represents the trivial orbit consisting of the zero element only.

nodes.name: Phi-mutation
nodes.statement: For each variety $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$ in (6.2) we shall define some transformations of chromosomes which we call $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$-mutations. A chromsome $X \in \boldsymbol{\Phi}$ is transformed by a $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$-mutation into another chromosome $Y \in \Phi$ such that $X \leqslant Y, X \neq Y$, and sig $X=\operatorname{sig} Y$. We shall indicate such a mutation symbolically by $X \rightarrow Y$.
nodes.statement_short: A Phi-mutation X -> Y transforms X into a strictly larger chromosome Y of Phi with the same signature.

nodes.name: Mutations are stable under adding chromosomes
nodes.statement: If $X \rightarrow Y$ is a $\Phi$-mutation and $Z \in \Phi$ then also $X+Z \rightarrow Y+Z$ is a $\Phi$-mutation. Conversely, if $X, Y, Z \in \Phi$ and $X+Z \rightarrow Y+Z$ is a $\Phi$-mutation then also $X \rightarrow Y$ is a $\Phi$-mutation.

nodes.name: Disjoint chromosomes
nodes.statement: Hence it suffices to list only the $\Phi$-mutations $X \rightarrow Y$ such that $X$ and $Y$ are disjoint, i.e., $X$ and $Y$ have no genes in common.

nodes.name: Primitive mutation
nodes.statement: Such $\Phi$-mutations we call primitive.

nodes.name: Primitive Pi-mutations
nodes.statement: The primitive $\Pi$-mutations are the following: \begin{equation*} g^{\varepsilon}(m)+g^{-\varepsilon}(n) \rightarrow g^{-\varepsilon}(m-1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+1), \quad m \leqslant n ; \tag{8.1} \end{equation*} \begin{gather*} g^{\varepsilon}(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n) \rightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m-2)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+2), \quad 1<m \leqslant n ; \tag{8.2}\\ g_{\varepsilon}(m)+g_{-\varepsilon}(n) \rightarrow g_{-\varepsilon}(m-1)+g_{\varepsilon}(n+1), \quad m \leqslant n ; \tag{8.3} \end{gather*} where $g_{\varepsilon}(n)=g^{(-1)^{n-1} \varepsilon}(n), \varepsilon= \pm$.
nodes.statement_short: Lists the three families (8.1)-(8.3) of primitive Pi-mutations, moving one or two boxes between two polarized genes.

nodes.name: Mutation (8.1)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} g^{\varepsilon}(m)+g^{-\varepsilon}(n) \rightarrow g^{-\varepsilon}(m-1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+1), \quad m \leqslant n ; \tag{8.1} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Mutation (8.2)
nodes.statement: g^{\varepsilon}(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n) \rightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m-2)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+2), \quad 1<m \leqslant n ; \tag{8.2}

nodes.name: Mutation (8.3)
nodes.statement: g_{\varepsilon}(m)+g_{-\varepsilon}(n) \rightarrow g_{-\varepsilon}(m-1)+g_{\varepsilon}(n+1), \quad m \leqslant n ; \tag{8.3}

nodes.name: Pi-mutations of g+(5)+g+(4)+g-(1)
nodes.statement: Example 3. If $X=g^{+}(5)+g^{+}(4)+g^{-}(1)$ and $X \rightarrow Y$ is a $\Pi$-mutation then $Y$ is one of the chormosomes $Y_{1}=g^{-}(6)+g^{+}(4), Y_{2}=g^{+}(5)+g^{-}(5), Y_{3}=g^{+}(6)+$ $g^{+}(3)+g^{-}(1)$, or $Y_{4}=g^{+}(6)+g^{+}(4)$. The mutations $X \rightarrow Y_{1}$ and $X \rightarrow Y_{2}$ are of type (8.1) while the mutations $X \rightarrow Y_{3}$ and $X \rightarrow Y_{4}$ are of type (8.3). (Since $X$ has three genes, none of these mutations is primitive.)

nodes.name: Primitive (Lambda,Pi)- and (Pi,Lambda)-mutations
nodes.statement: If $\boldsymbol{\Phi}=(\Lambda, \Pi)$ or $(\Pi, \Lambda)$ then the primitive $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$-mutations are the following: $$ \begin{array}{cc} g(m)+g(n) \rightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m-1)+g^{-\varepsilon}(n+1), & m \leqslant n ; \qquad\text{(8.4)} \\ g(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n) \rightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m-1)+g(n+1), & m<n ; \qquad\text{(8.5)} \\ g^{\varepsilon}(m)+g(n) \rightarrow g(m-1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+1), & m<n ; \qquad\text{(8.6)} \\ g^{\varepsilon}(m)+g^{-\varepsilon}(n) \rightarrow g(m-1)+g(n+1), & m \leqslant n ; \qquad\text{(8.7)} \\ g^{\varepsilon}(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n) \rightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m-2)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+2), & 1<m \leqslant n ; \qquad\text{(8.8)} \end{array} $$ where $\varepsilon= \pm$. It should be understood that if, say, $\Phi=(\Lambda, \Pi)$ then in (8.4) $m$ and $n$ are even positive integers, etc.
nodes.statement_short: Lists the five families (8.4)-(8.8) of primitive mutations for the mixed varieties (Lambda,Pi) and (Pi,Lambda).

nodes.name: Mutation (8.4)
nodes.statement: g(m)+g(n) \rightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m-1)+g^{-\varepsilon}(n+1), & m \leqslant n ; \qquad\text{(8.4)}

nodes.name: Mutation (8.5)
nodes.statement: g(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n) \rightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m-1)+g(n+1), & m<n ; \qquad\text{(8.5)}

nodes.name: Mutation (8.6)
nodes.statement: g^{\varepsilon}(m)+g(n) \rightarrow g(m-1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+1), & m<n ; \qquad\text{(8.6)}

nodes.name: Mutation (8.7)
nodes.statement: g^{\varepsilon}(m)+g^{-\varepsilon}(n) \rightarrow g(m-1)+g(n+1), & m \leqslant n ; \qquad\text{(8.7)}

nodes.name: Mutation (8.8)
nodes.statement: g^{\varepsilon}(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n) \rightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m-2)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+2), & 1<m \leqslant n ; \qquad\text{(8.8)}

nodes.name: Primitive (2Lambda,Pi)- and (Pi,2Lambda)-mutations
nodes.statement: Finally if $\Phi=(2 \Lambda, \Pi)$ or $(\Pi, 2 \Lambda)$ then the primitive $\Phi$-mutations are the following: (8.9) (8.10) (8.12) (8.14) (8.16) (8.17)\\ where $\varepsilon, \varepsilon^{\prime}= \pm$. It should be also understood that $g(0)$ and $g^{\varepsilon}(0), \varepsilon= \pm$, are zero chromosomes.

nodes.name: Enough Phi-mutations
nodes.statement: We say that there are enough $\Phi$-mutations if given $X, Y \in \Phi$, such that $X \leqslant Y$ and $\operatorname{sig} X=\operatorname{sig} Y$, there exists a finite chain of $\Phi$-mutations $$ X_{0} \rightarrow X_{1} \rightarrow X_{2} \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow X_{m} \quad(m \geqslant 0) $$ with $X_{0}=X$ and $X_{m}=Y$.

nodes.name: Enough mutations theorem
nodes.statement: Theorem 6. If $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$ is one of the varieties (6.2) then there are enough $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$-mutations.
also_stated_at: It says that if $X \leqslant Y$ in $\Phi_{j}$ then there exists a chain of $\Phi_{j}$-mutations $X_{0} \rightarrow X_{1} \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow X_{m}(m \geqslant 0)$ such that $X=X_{0}$ and $Y=X_{m}$.
conclusions: there are enough $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$-mutations
nodes.statement_short: In each of the five varieties, X <= Y with equal signatures is connected by a finite chain of mutations.

nodes.name: Proof of the sufficiency part of Theorem 5
nodes.statement:
Recall that $G$ is a classical group of the $j$ th series defined by a pair $(V, f)$ and $j \in\{4,6,7,9,10\}$. Let $\mathcal{O}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{O}_{2}$ be two nilpotent orbits of $G$ in its Lie algebra $L$. Let $X_{1}=X\left(\mathcal{O}_{1}ight)$ and $X_{2}=X\left(\mathcal{O}_{2}ight)$ be the corresponding chromosomes in $\Phi_{j}$. By hypothesis we have $X_{1} \leqslant X_{2}$. We also know that $\operatorname{sig} X_{1}=\operatorname{sig} X_{2}=\operatorname{sig}(f)$. We have to show that $\mathcal{O}_{1} \leqslant \mathcal{O}_{2}$, i.e., $\mathcal{O}_{1} \subset \overline{\mathcal{O}}_{2}$. By Theorem 6 it suffices to consider the case when  egin{equation*} X_{1} ightarrow X_{2} 	ag{9.1} \end{equation*} is a $\Phi_{j}$-mutation. Without any loss of generality we may (and we will) assume that this mutation is primitive. In order to prove that $\mathcal{O}_{1} \leqslant \mathcal{O}_{2}$ we shall construct a linear one-parameter family  egin{equation*} x(t)=x_{0}+t x_{1} 	ag{9.2} \end{equation*} in $L$ such that $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$ and $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ for $t>0$. (Only in one case we shall use a quadratic family.) Indeed the existence of such a family implies that $x_{0} \in  ar{	heta}_{2}$, and so $\mathcal{O}_{1} \subset \overline{\mathcal{O}}_{2}$. In order to verify that, say, $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$ it suffices to show that $\left(V, f, x_{0}ight) \in \Delta\left(\mathcal{O}_{1}ight)$. For this purpose we decompose $V$ into an orthogonal direct sum of $x_{0}$-invariant subspaces $V_{1}, \ldots, V_{k}$ so that the corresponding types $\Delta_{1}, \ldots, \Delta_{k}$ are indecomposable. We identify these indecomposable types by the criteria of §5 and verify that $\Delta\left(\mathcal{O}_{1}ight)=\Delta_{1}+\cdots+\Delta_{k}$. The same method is used to prove that $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ for $t>0$. We shall distinguish several cases according to the value of $j$.\ 10. The case $j=4$. We have $\Phi_{4}=\Pi$ and the primitive $\Pi$-mutations are defined by (8.1)-(8.3). These mutations can also be written as  egin{gather*} g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(n+1) ightarrow g^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+2), \quad n-m=2 k+1 ; 	ag{10.1}\ g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+1) ightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m-1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+3), \quad m \leqslant n ; 	ag{10.2}\ g^{-\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+1) ightarrow g^{-\varepsilon^{\prime}}(m)+g^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(n+2), \quad n-m=2 k ; 	ag{10.3} \end{gather*} where $k(\geqslant 0)$ is an integer and $\varepsilon, \varepsilon^{\prime}= \pm$.\ Indeed, (8.2) and (10.2) list the same mutations. Mutations (8.1) for $n-m$ even are the same as (10.3) for $\varepsilon^{\prime}=\varepsilon$. Mutations (8.1) for $n-m$ odd are the same as (10.1) for $\varepsilon^{\prime}=-\varepsilon$. Mutations (8.3) for $n-m$ even are the same as (10.3) for $\varepsilon^{\prime}=\varepsilon$. Finally, mutations (8.3) for $n-m$ odd are the same as (10.1) for $\varepsilon^{\prime}=\varepsilon$. Assume first that the mutation (9.1) is of the form (10.1). We can choose a basis $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{m}, e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{n}^{\prime}$ of $V$ such that  egin{equation*} f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0, \quad f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}ight)=\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m}, \quad f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=\varepsilon^{\prime} \delta_{r+s, n} 	ag{10.4} \end{equation*} holds for all relevant $r, s$. eq 0$. We have $$ x(t)^{n+2}=0 \quad 	ext { and } \quad x(t)^{n+1} e_{0}=2 t(-1)^{m+n^{\prime}}\left(-2 t e_{m+k-1}^{\prime}+e_{n}^{\prime \prime}ight) . $$ Hence $x(t)$ has a Jordan block of size $n+2$. But we know that such blocks must occur in pairs, and so there are two blocks of size $n+2$. Thus if $m=1$ then $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$. Now let $m \geqslant 2$. Since $\operatorname{dim} \operatorname{Ker} x(t)=3, x(t)$ consists of three Jordan blocks. Hence the remaining Jordan block has size $m-1$. By invoking the necessity part of Theorem 5 we can conclude that this block must be of type $\Delta_{m-2}^{-\varepsilon}(0)$. Therefore $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$. Finally, assume that the mutation (9.1) has the form  egin{equation*} 2 g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+2 g^{-\varepsilon}(n+1) ightarrow 2 g(m)+2 g(n+2), \quad m \leqslant n . 	ag{12.19} \end{equation*} Let $V=V_{1} \oplus V_{2}$ be an orthogonal decomposition with $V_{1}=W_{1} \oplus W_{1}^{\prime}$, $V_{2}=W_{2} \oplus W_{2}^{\prime}$ where $W_{1}, W_{1}^{\prime}, W_{2}, W_{2}^{\prime}$ are totally isotropic subspaces of dimension $m+k+1$ each $\left(k=n^{\prime}-m^{\prime}ight)$. We can choose bases $a_{0}, \ldots, a_{m+k} ; a_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, a_{m+k}^{\prime}$; $b_{0}, \ldots, b_{m+k}$; and $b_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, b_{m+k}^{\prime}$ of $W_{1}, W_{1}^{\prime}, W_{2}$, and $W_{2}^{\prime}$, respectively, such that $f\left(a_{r}, a_{s}^{\prime}ight)=f\left(b_{r}, b_{s}^{\prime}ight)=(-1)^{n-m^{\prime}+1} \varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m+k}$ for all $r, s$. Let $x_{0}$ be the operator in $V$ defined by $$  egin{aligned} & x_{0} a_{r}=a_{r+1} \quad 	ext { for } r 
eq k-1, k+m, \ & x^{0} a_{k-1}=a_{k}+(-1)^{m} a_{0}^{\prime} \quad 	ext { if } k>0, \ & x_{0} a_{k+m}=-a_{m+1}^{\prime} \quad\left(a_{m+1}^{\prime}=0 	ext { if } k=0ight), \ & x_{0} a_{r}^{\prime}=-a_{r+1}^{\prime} \quad(0 \leqslant r<m+k), \quad x_{0} a_{m+k}^{\prime}=0, \end{aligned} $$ and by analogous formulas obtained from these by replacing $a$ with $b$ everywhere. From the case (12.10) it follows that $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$. We make $V$ into a complex vector space by defining the action of $i$ by $i a_{r}=b_{r}$ and $i a_{r}^{\prime}=b_{r}^{\prime}$ for all $r$. We shall denote $V$ with this complex structure by $V^{\prime}$. Note that $a_{0}, \ldots, a_{m+k}, a_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, a_{m+k}^{\prime}$ is a basis of $V^{\prime}$. There exists a unique hermitian form $f^{\prime}$ on $V^{\prime}$ such that $\operatorname{Re} f^{\prime}=f$ for $j=6$ (then $f$ is symmetric) and $\operatorname{Im} f^{\prime}=f$ for $j=9$ (then $f$ is skew-symmetric). Indeed $f^{\prime}$ is determined by $$  egin{array}{ll} f^{\prime}\left(a_{r}, a_{s}ight)=f^{\prime}\left(a_{r}^{\prime}, a_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0, & \ f^{\prime}\left(a_{r}, a_{s}^{\prime}ight)=(-1)^{n-m^{\prime}+1} \varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m+k} & 	ext { if } j=6, \ f^{\prime}\left(a_{r}, a_{s}^{\prime}ight)=(-1)^{n-m^{\prime+1}} i \varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m+k} & 	ext { if } j=9 . \end{array} $$ It is clear that $f^{\prime}$ is nondegenerate and $\operatorname{sig}\left(f^{\prime}ight)=(k+m, k+m)$. Let $U$ be the classical group of the fourth series defined by the pair $\left(V^{\prime}, f^{\prime}ight)$. Clearly $U$ is a subgroup of $G$ and we shall view its Lie algebra $M$ as a subalgebra of $L$. Note that $x_{0}$ is a complex linear operator in $V^{\prime}$ and that $x_{0} \in M$. Let $Y_{1}=g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{-\varepsilon}(n+1)$ and $Y_{2}=g^{-\varepsilon}(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+2)$. Note that $\operatorname{sig} Y_{1}=\operatorname{sig} Y_{2}=(k+m, k+m)$. Let $\mathcal{O}_{r}^{\prime}(r=1,2)$ be the nilpotent orbit of $U$ in $M$ corresponding to the chromosome $Y_{r}$. Note that $x_{0}$ as a complex linear operator consists of two Jordan blocks whose sizes are $n+1$ and $m+1$. We claim that $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime}$. If $n=m$ this follows from the fact that $x_{0}$ has a totally isotropic Jordan block, for instance, its restriction to the subspace of $V^{\prime}$ spanned by the vectors $a_{r}$. Now let $k>0$. Then by using $x_{0}^{n} a_{0}=2(-1)^{k} a_{m+k}^{\prime}$ and (12.1) we find that $(-i)^{n}(-\varepsilon) f^{\prime}\left(a_{0}, x_{0}^{n} a_{0}ight)=2$, and so by (5.3) the larger block of $x_{0}$ is of type $\Delta_{n}^{-\varepsilon}(0)$. Similarly one can check that the other block is of type $\Delta_{m}^{\varepsilon}(0)$, and consequently\ $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime}$. This implies that $\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime} \subset \mathcal{O}_{1}$. On the other hand it is clear that $\mathcal{O}_{2}^{\prime} \subset \mathcal{O}_{2}$. Since $Y_{1} \leqslant Y_{2}$, we have $\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime} \leqslant \mathcal{O}_{2}^{\prime}$ by the case $j=4$ of Theorem 5. Consequently $\mathcal{O}_{1} \leqslant \mathcal{O}_{2}$. Since every primitive $(2 \Lambda, \Pi)$ or $(\Pi, 2 \Lambda)$-mutation has one of the forms (12.2), (12.3), (12.6), (12.7), (12.9), (12.10), (12.12), (12.16), or (12.19), the proof of Theorem 5 is completed.
nodes.statement_short: By Theorem 6 reduce to one primitive mutation and exhibit a linear family x0 + t x1 with x0 in O1 and x(t) in O2 for t>0. Cases j=7,10 reduce to j=4 by quaternionic extension (Lemmas 7, 8); j=6,9 are done case by case.

nodes.name: Mutation X1 -> X2
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} X_{1} \rightarrow X_{2} \tag{9.1} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Linear one-parameter family x(t)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} x(t)=x_{0}+t x_{1} \tag{9.2} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Mutation (10.1)
nodes.statement: g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(n+1) \rightarrow g^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+2), \quad n-m=2 k+1 ; \tag{10.1}

nodes.name: Mutation (10.2)
nodes.statement: g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+1) \rightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m-1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+3), \quad m \leqslant n ; \tag{10.2}

nodes.name: Mutation (10.3)
nodes.statement: g^{-\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+1) \rightarrow g^{-\varepsilon^{\prime}}(m)+g^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(n+2), \quad n-m=2 k ; \tag{10.3}

nodes.name: Equation (10.4)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}\right)=0, \quad f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}\right)=\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m}, \quad f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}\right)=\varepsilon^{\prime} \delta_{r+s, n} \tag{10.4} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Equation (10.5)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}\right)=f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}\right)=0, \quad f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}\right)=\delta_{r+s, m+k} \tag{10.5} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Equation (10.6)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} \varepsilon(-i)^{m} f\left(e_{0}+\lambda e_{0}^{\prime}, x_{0}^{m}\left(e_{0}+\lambda e_{0}^{\prime}\right)\right)=2 \varepsilon \lambda, \tag{10.6} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Equation (10.7)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} x(t)^{n+1} e_{0}=2 i^{n+1} \varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m+k}^{\prime}, \quad x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}=0 . \tag{10.7} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Equation (10.8)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} x(t)^{m-1} a=i^{m-1}\left(e_{m+k}-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m-1}^{\prime}-\varepsilon e_{m}^{\prime}\right), \quad x(t)^{m} a=0 . \tag{10.8} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Mutations of (Pi,Lambda) and (Lambda,Pi) come from Pi-mutations
nodes.statement: Lemma 7. Every primitive $(\Pi, \Lambda)$-mutation, resp. $(\Lambda, \Pi)$-mutation, is of the form $\sigma(X) \rightarrow \sigma(Y)$, resp. $\tau(X) \rightarrow \tau(Y)$, for a suitable primitive $\Pi$-mutation $X \rightarrow Y$.
conclusions: Every primitive $(\Pi, \Lambda)$-mutation, resp. $(\Lambda, \Pi)$-mutation, is of the form $\sigma(X) \rightarrow \sigma(Y)$, resp. $\tau(X) \rightarrow \tau(Y)$, for a suitable primitive $\Pi$-mutation $X \rightarrow Y$.
nodes.statement_short: Every primitive (Pi,Lambda)- or (Lambda,Pi)-mutation is the image under sigma or tau of a primitive Pi-mutation.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7
nodes.statement: Proof. We have to show that each of the mutations (8.4)-(8.8) can be obtained by applying $\sigma$ or $\tau$ to a primitive $\Pi$-mutation $X \rightarrow Y$. In the case (8.4) we take $X=g^{-\varepsilon}(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n), \quad Y$ is determined by (8.4). In the case (8.5) we take $X=g^{-\varepsilon}(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n), \quad Y=g^{\varepsilon}(m-1)+g^{-\varepsilon}(n+1)$. In the case (8.6) we take $X=g^{\varepsilon}(m)+g^{-\varepsilon}(n), \quad Y=g^{-\varepsilon}(m-1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+1)$. In the case (8.7) we take $Y=g^{-\varepsilon}(m-1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+1), X$ being already determined by (8.7). The mutations (8.8) are also primitive $\Pi$-mutations.
nodes.statement_short: Case check over (8.4)-(8.8): for each family exhibit a primitive Pi-mutation whose image under sigma or tau is it.

nodes.name: Chromosomes after quaternionic extension
nodes.statement: Lemma 8. With the above notation we have $X_{\sigma}=\sigma(X)$ and $X_{\tau}=\tau(X)$.
conclusions: $X_{\sigma}=\sigma(X)$ and $X_{\tau}=\tau(X)$
nodes.statement_short: Extending a U(p,q) nilpotent element to the quaternionic groups of series 7 and 10 maps its chromosome X to sigma(X), resp. tau(X).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8
nodes.statement: Proof. It suffices to prove this when $\Delta$ is indecomposable, i.e., $X$ is a gene, say $X=g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)$. We may assume (see §5) that there is a basis $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{m}$ of $W$ such that \begin{equation*} g\left(e_{r}, e_{s}\right)=\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m} \tag{11.1} \end{equation*} for all $r, s$ and \begin{equation*} x e_{r}=e_{r+1} i \quad(0 \leqslant r<m), \quad x e_{m}=0 . \tag{11.2} \end{equation*} Since $W^{\prime}$ is indecomposable with respect to $x$, we must have $X_{\sigma}=g(m+1)$ for $m$ even and $X_{\tau}=g(m+1)$ for $m$ odd. If $m$ is odd we have $i^{m-1} \varepsilon g_{\sigma}\left(e_{0}, x^{m} e_{0}\right)=$ $-i^{m} \varepsilon g\left(e_{0}, e_{m} i^{m}\right)=1$ by (11.1), (11.2) and the definition of $g_{\sigma}$. By (5.5) we have\\ $X_{\sigma}=g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)$ in this case. If $m$ is even then $i^{m} \varepsilon g_{\tau}\left(e_{0}, x^{m} e_{0}\right)=i^{m} \varepsilon g\left(e_{0}, e_{m} i^{m}\right)=1$, and so by (5.4) we have $X_{\tau}=g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)$. Thus $X_{\sigma}=\sigma(X)$ and $X_{\tau}=\tau(X)$ in all cases.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to one gene, use the model basis of Section 5 and the sign inequalities (5.4), (5.5) according to the parity of m.

nodes.name: Equation (11.1)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} g\left(e_{r}, e_{s}\right)=\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m} \tag{11.1} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Equation (11.2)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} x e_{r}=e_{r+1} i \quad(0 \leqslant r<m), \quad x e_{m}=0 . \tag{11.2} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Sign identity for m'
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} (-1)^{m-m^{\prime}}= \begin{cases}i^{m} & \text { if } m \text { is even, } \\ i^{m-1} & \text { if } m \text { is odd. }\end{cases} \tag{12.1} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Mutation (12.2)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} 2 g(m+1) \rightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m)+g^{-\varepsilon}(m+2) \text {. } \tag{12.2} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Equation (12.3)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} x(t)^{m+1} e_{0}=-2 \varepsilon(-1)^{m^{\prime}} t e_{m}^{\prime} \quad \text { and } \quad-\varepsilon i^{2 m^{\prime}} f\left(e_{0}, x(t)^{m+1} e_{0}\right)=2 t . \tag{12.3} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Mutation (12.4)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(n+1) \rightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m-1)+g^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(n+3), \quad m \leqslant n . \tag{12.4} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Equation (12.5)
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} & x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}=-\varepsilon \varepsilon^{\prime}(-1)^{n-n^{\prime}} t^{2} e_{m}, \quad \text { and } \\ & \varepsilon^{\prime}(-1)^{n-n^{\prime}+1} f\left(e_{0}, x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}\right)=t^{2} . \tag{12.5} \end{align*}

nodes.name: Mutation (12.6)
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{+}(n & +1)+g^{-}(n+1) \\ & \rightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m-1)+2 g(n+2), \quad m \leqslant n . \tag{12.6} \end{align*}

nodes.name: Mutation (12.7)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} g^{+}(m+1)+g^{-}(m+1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+1) \rightarrow 2 g(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+3), \quad m \leqslant n . \tag{12.7} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Equation (12.8)
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} & x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}=(-1)^{n-n^{\prime+1}} \varepsilon t^{2} e_{m}, \quad \text { and } \\ & \varepsilon(-1)^{n-n^{\prime}+1} f\left(e_{0}, x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}\right)=t^{2} . \tag{12.8} \end{align*}

nodes.name: Mutation (12.9)
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} g^{+}(m+1)+g^{-}(m+1)+g^{+}(n+1)+g^{-}(n+1) &\\ \rightarrow 2 g(m)+2 g(n+2), \quad m \leqslant n . & \tag{12.9}\end{align*}

nodes.name: Mutation (12.10)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{-\varepsilon}(n+1) \rightarrow g^{-\varepsilon}(m-1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+3), \quad m \leqslant n . \tag{12.10} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Equation (12.11)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} \varepsilon(-1)^{n-n^{\prime}+1} f\left(e_{0}, x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}\right)>0 . \tag{12.11} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Mutation (12.12)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} 2 g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{-\varepsilon}(n+1) \rightarrow 2 g(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+3), \quad m<n . \tag{12.12} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Equation (12.13)
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} & x_{0}^{n} e_{0}=-2(-1)^{m+n^{\prime}} e_{k+m}^{\prime}, \quad x_{0} e_{k+m}^{\prime}=0, \\ & -\varepsilon(-1)^{n-n^{\prime}} f\left(e_{0}, x_{0}^{n} e_{0}\right)=2 . \tag{12.13} \end{align*}

nodes.name: Equation (12.14)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} x_{0}^{m} a=b, \quad x_{0} b=0, \quad \varepsilon(-1)^{m-m^{\prime}} f\left(a, x_{0}^{m} a\right)=2 . \tag{12.14} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Equation (12.15)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}=-(-1)^{k+m-m^{\prime}} t^{2} e_{k+m}^{\prime}, \quad \varepsilon(-1)^{n-n^{\prime}+1} f\left(e_{0}, x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}\right)=t^{2} . \tag{12.15} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Mutation (12.16)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+2 g^{-\varepsilon}(n+1) \rightarrow g^{-\varepsilon}(m-1)+2 g(n+2), \quad m<n . \tag{12.16} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Equation (12.17)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} -\varepsilon(-1)^{n-n^{\prime}} f\left(e_{0}, x_{0}^{n} e_{0}\right)=2 . \tag{12.17} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Equation (12.18)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} \varepsilon(-1)^{m-m^{\prime}} f\left(a, x_{0}^{m} a\right)=2 . \tag{12.18} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Mutation (12.19)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} 2 g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+2 g^{-\varepsilon}(n+1) \rightarrow 2 g(m)+2 g(n+2), \quad m \leqslant n . \tag{12.19} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Multiplicative Jordan decomposition
nodes.statement: Each $x \in G$ has a unique multiplicative Jordan decomposition $x=x_{s} x_{u}$, where $x_{s}$ is semisimple, $x_{u}$ is unipotent, both $x_{s}$ and $x_{u}$ are in $G$, and $x_{s} x_{u}=x_{u} x_{s}$.

nodes.name: Semisimple and unipotent components
nodes.statement: We refer to $x_{s}$ (resp. $x_{u}$ ) as the semisimple (resp. unipotent) component of $x$.

nodes.name: Generalized eigenspace V(lambda, x) in G
nodes.statement: For $x \in G$ and $\lambda \in \mathbf{C}^{*}$ let $$ V(\lambda, x)=\operatorname{Ker}(x-\lambda)^{\infty} $$ if $\mathbf{F}=\mathbf{C}$. Otherwise let $$ V(\lambda, x)=\operatorname{Ker}\left(x^{2}-2 \operatorname{Re}(\lambda) x+|\lambda|^{2}\right)^{\infty} . $$

nodes.name: Isotropy of V(lambda, x)
nodes.statement: If $j \in\{5,8\}$ and $\lambda \neq \pm 1$ or $j \in\{4,6,7,9,10\}$ and $|\lambda| \neq 1$ then $V(\lambda, x)$ is totally isotropic.
conclusions: $V(\lambda, x)$ is totally isotropic

nodes.name: Subspace V'(lambda, x)
nodes.statement: This leads us to define the subspace $V^{\prime}(\lambda, x)$ by $$ V^{\prime}(\lambda, x)=\left\{\begin{array}{l} V(\lambda, x) \quad \text { for } j \in\{1,2,3\}, \\ V(\lambda, x)+V\left(\lambda^{-1}, x\right) \quad \text { for } j \in\{5,8\}, \\ V(\lambda, x)+V\left(\bar{\lambda}^{-1}, x\right) \quad \text { for } j \in\{4,6,7,9,10\} . \end{array}\right. $$

nodes.name: V'(lambda, x) nondegenerate and orthogonal
nodes.statement: If $4 \leqslant j \leqslant 10$ the subspaces $V^{\prime}(\lambda, x)$ are nondegenerate and orthogonal to each other.
conclusions: the subspaces $V^{\prime}(\lambda, x)$ are nondegenerate and orthogonal to each other

nodes.name: Index set Omega*_j and decomposition (13.1)
nodes.statement: We obtain a direct (and orthogonal if $j \geqslant 4$ ) decomposition \begin{equation*} V=\sum_{\lambda \in \Omega_{j}^{*}} V^{\prime}(\lambda, x) \tag{13.1} \end{equation*} where $\Omega_{j}^{*}$ is a subset of $\mathbf{C}^{*}$ specified by the Table V. \begin{table}[h] \begin{center} \begin{tabular}[t]{|l|l|} \hline $j$ & $\Omega_{j}^{*}$ \\ \hline 1 & C* \\ \hline 2,3 & $\operatorname{Im} \lambda \geqslant 0$ \\ \hline 4 & $|\lambda| \geqslant 1$ \\ \hline 5,8 & $\operatorname{Im} \lambda>0$ or $\left(\lambda \in \mathbf{R}^{*} \&|\lambda| \geqslant 1\right)$ \\ \hline 6, 7, 9, 10 & $\operatorname{Im} \lambda \geqslant 0 \&|\lambda| \geqslant 1$ \\ \hline \end{tabular} \captionsetup{labelformat=empty} \caption{Table V} \end{center} \end{table}

nodes.name: Decomposition of V into V'(lambda, x)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} V=\sum_{\lambda \in \Omega_{j}^{*}} V^{\prime}(\lambda, x) \tag{13.1} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Restrictions x_lambda and x'_lambda
nodes.statement: For $\lambda \in \mathbf{C}^{*}$ let $x_{\lambda}$ (resp. $x_{\lambda}^{\prime}$ ) be the restriction of $x$ to $V(\lambda, x)$ (resp. $V^{\prime}(\lambda, x)$ ).

nodes.name: Classical group G(lambda, x)
nodes.statement: If $1 \leqslant j \leqslant 3$ let $G(\lambda, x)$ be the general linear group of the space $V(\lambda, x)$. If $4 \leqslant j \leqslant 10$ let $G(\lambda, x)$ be the classical group defined by the subspace $V^{\prime}(\lambda, x)$ and the restriction of the form $f$ to this subspace. Thus in all cases $G(\lambda, x)$ is also a classical group of the $j$ th series. Clearly $x_{\lambda}^{\prime} \in G(\lambda, x)$ for all $\lambda$.

nodes.name: Centralizer C(lambda, x)
nodes.statement: We denote by $C(\lambda, x)$ the centralizer of $x_{\lambda}^{\prime}$ in $G(\lambda, x)$.

nodes.name: Centralizer as product of C(lambda, x)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} C_{G}(x)=\prod_{\lambda \in \Omega_{j}^{*}} C(\lambda, x) . \tag{13.2} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Centralizer Theorem for semisimple elements of G
nodes.statement: Theorem 1'. Let $G$ be a classical group of the jth series and $x \in G$ a semisimple element. Then each $C(\lambda, x)$ in (13.2) is a classical group of kth series where $k$ depends only on $j$ and $\lambda$ and is specified in the last column of Table III.
assumptions: Let $G$ be a classical group of the jth series and $x \in G$ a semisimple element.
conclusions: each $C(\lambda, x)$ in (13.2) is a classical group of kth series where $k$ depends only on $j$ and $\lambda$ and is specified in the last column of Table III

nodes.name: Conjugation action a.x
nodes.statement: The group $G$ acts on itself by conjugation. We shall write $a \cdot x=a x a^{-1}$ for the result of the action of the element $a$ on $x \in G$.

nodes.name: Conjugacy class G.x
nodes.statement: Then $G \cdot x=\left\{a x a^{-1}: a \in G\right\}$ is the conjugacy class of $x$ in $G$.

nodes.name: Reduction theorem for closures of conjugacy classes
nodes.statement: Theorem 2'. Let $G$ be a classical group, $x, y \in G$ and $x=x_{s} x_{u}$ the Jordan decomposition of $x$. Then $y \in \overline{G \cdot x}$ iff $a \cdot y=x_{s} z$ for some $a \in G$ and some \begin{equation*} z \in \overline{C_{G}\left(x_{s}\right) \cdot x_{u}} . \tag{13.3} \end{equation*}
assumptions: Let $G$ be a classical group, $x, y \in G$ and $x=x_{s} x_{u}$ the Jordan decomposition of $x$.
conclusions: Then $y \in \overline{G \cdot x}$ iff $a \cdot y=x_{s} z$ for some $a \in G$ and some
equivalent_conditions: $a \cdot y=x_{s} z$ for some $a \in G$ and some

nodes.name: Closure condition on z (group case)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} z \in \overline{C_{G}\left(x_{s}\right) \cdot x_{u}} . \tag{13.3} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Reduction to unipotent classes
nodes.statement: This theorem reduces the problem of closures of conjugacy classes to the case of unipotent conjugacy classes. For this reason we shall now restrict our attention only to unipotent conjugacy classes.

nodes.name: Exponential map identifies nilpotent and unipotent elements
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be the Lie algebra of $G$ and $\exp : L \rightarrow G$ the exponential map of $G$. It is known that exp induces a $G$-equivariant homeomorphism of the set of nilpotent elements of $L$ with the set of unipotent elements of $G$. (In particular, there is a bijection between the nilpotent orbits of $G$ in $L$ and the unipotent conjugacy classes of $G$.)
assumptions: Let $L$ be the Lie algebra of $G$ and $\exp : L \rightarrow G$ the exponential map of $G$.
conclusions: exp induces a $G$-equivariant homeomorphism of the set of nilpotent elements of $L$ with the set of unipotent elements of $G$

nodes.name: Closures of conjugacy classes are determined
nodes.statement: This clearly solves the problem of closures of conjugacy classes of $G$.
conclusions: This clearly solves the problem of closures of conjugacy classes of $G$.

nodes.name: Diagram of a chromosome
nodes.statement: It is convenient to represent chromosomes by diagrams. For instance the chromosome $$ X=2 g(3)+g^{-}(2)+g(2)+g^{+}(4) $$ can be represented by the diagram\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{3049372b-fe1b-4647-987b-29640168b2a6-27_247_200_1942_356}\\ \includegraphics[max width=\textwidth, alt={}, center]{3049372b-fe1b-4647-987b-29640168b2a6-27_247_202_1942_1023} The rows of such diagrams can be permuted arbitrarily (they correspond to the constituent genes of $X$ ). We shall usually arrange rows in decreasing rank as in the second diagram above.

nodes.name: Priming deletes the first column
nodes.statement: It is clear that the diagram of $X^{\prime}$ can be obtained from the diagram of $X$ by deleting its first column.
conclusions: the diagram of $X^{\prime}$ can be obtained from the diagram of $X$ by deleting its first column

nodes.name: Primed variety Phi'
nodes.statement: The priming operation can be extended to varieties. Thus if $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$ is a variety then $\Phi^{\prime}=\left\{X^{\prime}: X \in \Phi\right\}$ is also a variety.

nodes.name: Iterated primed varieties Phi^(k)
nodes.statement: By iterating, we obtain the varieties $\Phi^{(k)}, k \geqslant 0$, where $\Phi^{(0)}=\Phi, \Phi^{(1)}=\Phi^{\prime}$, etc.

nodes.name: Primes of the standard varieties
nodes.statement: For instance we have $\Lambda^{\prime}=\Lambda, \Pi^{\prime}=\Pi,(2 \Lambda, \Lambda)^{\prime}=(\Lambda, 2 \Lambda),(\Lambda, 2 \Lambda)^{\prime}=(2 \Lambda, \Lambda)$, $(\Lambda, \Pi)^{\prime}=(\Pi, \Lambda),(\Pi, \Lambda)^{\prime}=(\Lambda, \Pi),(2 \Lambda, \Pi)^{\prime}=(\Pi, 2 \Lambda)$, and $(\Pi, 2 \Lambda)^{\prime}=$ $(2 \Lambda, \Pi)$.

nodes.name: Lifting property
nodes.statement: Lemma 9 (lifting property). Let $\Phi$ be one of the varieties (6.2). If $X \in \Phi$ and $X^{(k)} \rightarrow U$ is a $\Phi^{(k)}$-mutation, then there exists a $\Phi$-mutation $X \rightarrow Z$ such that $Z^{(k)}=U$ and $\operatorname{sig} X^{(i)}=\operatorname{sig} Z^{(i)}$ for $0 \leqslant i \leqslant k$.
assumptions: Let $\Phi$ be one of the varieties (6.2).
conclusions: there exists a $\Phi$-mutation $X \rightarrow Z$ such that $Z^{(k)}=U$ and $\operatorname{sig} X^{(i)}=\operatorname{sig} Z^{(i)}$ for $0 \leqslant i \leqslant k$
nodes.statement_short: A mutation of the k-th prime X^(k) lifts to a mutation of X preserving the signatures of the first k primes.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 9
nodes.statement: Proof. It suffices to consider the case when $X^{(k)} \rightarrow U$ is a primitive $\Phi^{(k)}$-mutation and $X^{(k)}$ has the same number of genes (counting multiplicities) as $X$. The rest of the proof consists in routine verifications. We shall give the details only in the case when $X^{(k)} \rightarrow U$ is given by the formula (8.17), i.e., $$ X^{(k)}=g^{\varepsilon}(m)+2 g^{-\varepsilon}(n), \quad U=g^{-\varepsilon}(m-2)+2 g(n+1), $$ where $1<m \leqslant n$ and $\varepsilon= \pm$. Note that $\Phi^{(k)}=(\Pi, 2 \Lambda)$ if $m$ and $n$ are even and $\Phi^{(k)}=(2 \Lambda, \Pi)$ when they are odd. (It is understood in (8.17) that $n-m$ is even.) Hence $\Phi=(\Pi, 2 \Lambda)$ if $m-k$ is even and $\Phi=(2 \Lambda, \Pi)$ if $m-k$ is odd. Since we assume that $X$ and $X^{(k)}$ have the same number of genes, we must have $X=$ $g^{\varepsilon}(m+k)+2 g^{-\varepsilon}(n+k)$. We claim that the $\Phi$-mutation $X \rightarrow Z$ where $$ Z=g^{-\varepsilon}(m+k-2)+2 g(n+k+1) $$ has the desired properties. Indeed it is easy to check that $\operatorname{sig} X^{(i)}=\operatorname{sig} Z^{(i)}$ for $0 \leqslant i \leqslant k$ and it is obvious that $Z^{(k)}=U$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to primitive mutations with the same number of genes; routine verification, shown for (8.17) by adding k to every rank.

nodes.name: Lifting of a mutation
nodes.statement: The $\Phi$-mutation $X \rightarrow Z$ having the properties mentioned in Lemma 9 will be called a lifting of the $\Phi^{(k)}$-mutation $X^{(k)} \rightarrow U$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the rank: for X < Y produce a mutation X -> Z with Z <= Y. Reductions via disjointness and the lifting property (Lemma 9), then case analysis on the minimal-rank gene for each variety.

nodes.name: Signature matrix sigma(X)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} \sigma(X)=\left(\begin{array}{lll} a_{0} & a_{1} & a_{2} \cdots \\ b_{0} & b_{1} & b_{2} \cdots \end{array}\right) \tag{15.1} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Equation (15.2)
nodes.statement: a_{0} \geqslant a_{1} \geqslant a_{2} \geqslant \ldots, \quad a_{k}=0 \quad \text { for large } k ; \tag{15.2}

nodes.name: Equation (15.3)
nodes.statement: b_{0} \geqslant b_{1} \geqslant b_{2} \geqslant \ldots, \quad b_{k}=0 \quad \text { for large } k ; \tag{15.3}

nodes.name: Equation (15.4)
nodes.statement: \quad a_{0} \geqslant b_{1} \geqslant a_{2} \geqslant b_{3} \geqslant \ldots ; \tag{15.4}

nodes.name: Equation (15.5)
nodes.statement: \quad b_{0} \geqslant a_{1} \geqslant b_{2} \geqslant a_{3} \geqslant \ldots ; \tag{15.5}

nodes.name: Equation (15.6)
nodes.statement: a_{0}-a_{1} \geqslant b_{1}-b_{2} \geqslant a_{2}-a_{3} \geqslant b_{3}-b_{4} \geqslant \ldots ; \tag{15.6}

nodes.name: Equation (15.7)
nodes.statement: b_{0}-b_{1} \geqslant a_{1}-a_{2} \geqslant b_{2}-b_{3} \geqslant a_{3}-a_{4} \geqslant \ldots . \tag{15.7}

nodes.name: Equation (15.8)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} a_{k} \leqslant c_{k}, \quad b_{k} \leqslant d_{k} \quad(k \geqslant 0) . \tag{15.8} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Equation (15.9)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} Y^{(k)} \neq 0 \& k \geqslant 1 \Rightarrow a_{k}<c_{k} \text { or } b_{k}<d_{k} . \tag{15.9} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Equation (15.10)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} X \not \supset g^{+}(k)+g^{-}(k), \quad k \geqslant 1 . \tag{15.10} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Equation (16.1)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} Y^{(i)} \neq 0 \& i \geqslant 1 \Rightarrow r_{i}<s_{i} . \tag{16.1} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Equation (17.1)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} Y^{(i)} \neq 0 \& i \geqslant 1 \Rightarrow r_{i}<s_{i} . \tag{17.1} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Fix orbits O1 in the closure of O2
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{O}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{O}_{2}$ be $G$-orbits in $L$. Assume that $\mathcal{O}_{1} \subset \overline{\mathcal{O}}_{2}$, which we shall also write as $\mathcal{O}_{1} \leqslant \mathcal{O}_{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix orbits O1 in the closure of O2

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 2 to choose x, y with y = x_s + z
nodes.statement: By Theorem 2 we can choose $x \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ and $y \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$ such that $y=x_{s}+z$ and $z$ satisfies (3.1). Clearly, $z$ is the nilpotent part of $y, z=y_{n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 2 to choose x, y with y = x_s + z

nodes.name: Factor C_G(x_s) by Theorem 1
nodes.statement: By Theorem 1 we have \begin{equation*} C_{G}\left(x_{s}\right)=C\left(\zeta_{1}, x_{s}\right) \times \cdots \times C\left(\zeta_{m}, x_{s}\right) \tag{3.2} \end{equation*} where $\zeta_{1}, \ldots, \zeta_{m}$ are the distinct eigenvalues of $x_{s}$ belonging to $\Omega_{j}$.
nodes.statement_short: Factor C_G(x_s) by Theorem 1

nodes.name: Introduce the centralizer Lie algebras Z_L(x_s), Z(zeta_k, x
nodes.statement: Let $Z_{I}\left(x_{s}\right)$ be the centralizer of $x_{s}$ in $L$, i.e., $Z_{L}\left(x_{s}\right)=\left\{t \in L:\left[t, x_{s}\right]=0\right\}$.\\ We denote by $L\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$ the Lie algebra of $G\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$, and let $Z\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$ be the centralizer in $L\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$ of the restriction of $x_{s}$ to $V^{\prime}\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$. It is clear that $Z_{L}\left(x_{s}\right)$ is the Lie algebra of $C_{G}\left(x_{s}\right)$, and $Z\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$ is the Lie algebra of $C\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the centralizer Lie algebras Z_L(x_s), Z(zeta_k, x_s)

nodes.name: Decompose Z_L(x_s) as a direct sum
nodes.statement: It follows from (3.2) that \begin{equation*} Z_{L}\left(x_{s}\right)=Z\left(\zeta_{1}, x_{s}\right) \oplus \cdots \oplus Z\left(\zeta_{m}, x_{s}\right) . \tag{3.3} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Decompose Z_L(x_s) as a direct sum

nodes.name: Decompose x_n and z into components
nodes.statement: Since $x_{n}, z \in Z_{L}\left(x_{s}\right)$, we have $$ x_{n}=x_{n}^{(1)}+\cdots+x_{n}^{(m)}, \quad z=z^{(1)}+\cdots+z^{(m)}, $$ where $x_{n}^{(k)}, z^{(k)} \in Z\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right)$ for $1 \leqslant k \leqslant m$.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose x_n and z into components

nodes.name: Componentwise closure condition
nodes.statement: It follows from (3.1) to (3.3) that $z^{(k)} \in \overline{C\left(\zeta_{k}, x_{s}\right) \cdot x_{n}^{(k)}}, 1 \leqslant k \leqslant m$.
nodes.statement_short: Componentwise closure condition

nodes.name: Section 9: reduce to a primitive mutation and describe the d
nodes.statement: Recall that $G$ is a classical group of the $j$ th series defined by a pair $(V, f)$ and $j \in\{4,6,7,9,10\}$. Let $\mathcal{O}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{O}_{2}$ be two nilpotent orbits of $G$ in its Lie algebra $L$. Let $X_{1}=X\left(\mathcal{O}_{1}\right)$ and $X_{2}=X\left(\mathcal{O}_{2}\right)$ be the corresponding chromosomes in $\Phi_{j}$. By hypothesis we have $X_{1} \leqslant X_{2}$. We also know that $\operatorname{sig} X_{1}=\operatorname{sig} X_{2}=\operatorname{sig}(f)$. We have to show that $\mathcal{O}_{1} \leqslant \mathcal{O}_{2}$, i.e., $\mathcal{O}_{1} \subset \overline{\mathcal{O}}_{2}$. By Theorem 6 it suffices to consider the case when \begin{equation*} X_{1} \rightarrow X_{2} \tag{9.1} \end{equation*} is a $\Phi_{j}$-mutation. Without any loss of generality we may (and we will) assume that this mutation is primitive. In order to prove that $\mathcal{O}_{1} \leqslant \mathcal{O}_{2}$ we shall construct a linear one-parameter family \begin{equation*} x(t)=x_{0}+t x_{1} \tag{9.2} \end{equation*} in $L$ such that $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$ and $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ for $t>0$. (Only in one case we shall use a quadratic family.) Indeed the existence of such a family implies that $x_{0} \in \bar{\theta}_{2}$, and so $\mathcal{O}_{1} \subset \overline{\mathcal{O}}_{2}$. In order to verify that, say, $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$ it suffices to show that $\left(V, f, x_{0}\right) \in \Delta\left(\mathcal{O}_{1}\right)$. For this purpose we decompose $V$ into an orthogonal direct sum of $x_{0}$-invariant subspaces $V_{1}, \ldots, V_{k}$ so that the corresponding types $\Delta_{1}, \ldots, \Delta_{k}$ are indecomposable. We identify these indecomposable types by the criteria of §5 and verify that $\Delta\left(\mathcal{O}_{1}\right)=\Delta_{1}+\cdots+\Delta_{k}$. The same method is used to prove that $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ for $t>0$. We shall distinguish several cases according to the value of $j$.
nodes.statement_short: Section 9: reduce to a primitive mutation and describe the deformation method

nodes.name: By Theorem 6 reduce to a single primitive mutation X1 -> X2
nodes.statement: Recall that $G$ is a classical group of the $j$ th series defined by a pair $(V, f)$ and $j \in\{4,6,7,9,10\}$. nodes.name: A family x0 + t x1 with x0 in O1, x(t) in O2 suffices
nodes.statement: In order to prove that $\mathcal{O}_{1} \leqslant \mathcal{O}_{2}$ we shall construct a linear one-parameter family \begin{equation*} x(t)=x_{0}+t x_{1} \tag{9.2} \end{equation*} in $L$ such that $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$ and $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ for $t>0$. (Only in one case we shall use a quadratic family.) Indeed the existence of such a family implies that $x_{0} \in \bar{\theta}_{2}$, and so $\mathcal{O}_{1} \subset \overline{\mathcal{O}}_{2}$.
