nodes.name: Identify orbits by decomposing into indecomposable types
nodes.statement: In order to verify that, say, $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$ it suffices to show that $\left(V, f, x_{0}\right) \in \Delta\left(\mathcal{O}_{1}\right)$. For this purpose we decompose $V$ into an orthogonal direct sum of $x_{0}$-invariant subspaces $V_{1}, \ldots, V_{k}$ so that the corresponding types $\Delta_{1}, \ldots, \Delta_{k}$ are indecomposable. nodes.name: Section 10: the case j=4
nodes.statement:
10. The case $j=4$. We have $\Phi_{4}=\Pi$ and the primitive $\Pi$-mutations are defined by (8.1)-(8.3). These mutations can also be written as  egin{gather*} g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(n+1) ightarrow g^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+2), \quad n-m=2 k+1 ; 	ag{10.1}\ g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+1) ightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m-1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+3), \quad m \leqslant n ; 	ag{10.2}\ g^{-\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+1) ightarrow g^{-\varepsilon^{\prime}}(m)+g^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(n+2), \quad n-m=2 k ; 	ag{10.3} \end{gather*} where $k(\geqslant 0)$ is an integer and $\varepsilon, \varepsilon^{\prime}= \pm$.\ Indeed, (8.2) and (10.2) list the same mutations. Mutations (8.1) for $n-m$ even are the same as (10.3) for $\varepsilon^{\prime}=\varepsilon$. Mutations (8.1) for $n-m$ odd are the same as (10.1) for $\varepsilon^{\prime}=-\varepsilon$. Mutations (8.3) for $n-m$ even are the same as (10.3) for $\varepsilon^{\prime}=\varepsilon$. Finally, mutations (8.3) for $n-m$ odd are the same as (10.1) for $\varepsilon^{\prime}=\varepsilon$. Assume first that the mutation (9.1) is of the form (10.1). We can choose a basis $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{m}, e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{n}^{\prime}$ of $V$ such that  egin{equation*} f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0, \quad f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}ight)=\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m}, \quad f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=\varepsilon^{\prime} \delta_{r+s, n} 	ag{10.4} \end{equation*} holds for all relevant $r, s$. We define linear maps $x_{0}$ and $x_{1}$ on $V$ by specifying their effect on basis elements: $$  egin{array}{ll} x_{0} e_{r}=i e_{r+1} & (0 \leqslant r<m), \quad x_{0} e_{m}=0, \ x_{0} e_{r}^{\prime}=i e_{r+1}^{\prime} & (0 \leqslant r<n), \quad x_{0} e_{n}^{\prime}=0, \end{array} $$ $$  egin{aligned} & x_{1} e_{r}=0 \quad(0 \leqslant r<m), \quad x_{1} e_{m}=i e_{n-k}^{\prime}, \ & x_{1} e_{r}^{\prime}=0 \quad 	ext { for } r

It is clear that $V=V_{1} \oplus V_{2}$, $\operatorname{dim} V_{1}=n+2, \operatorname{dim} V_{2}=m$. Note that the vectors $e_{r}-t e_{r+k}^{\prime}(1 \leqslant r \leqslant m)$ form a basis of $V_{2}$ and are orthogonal to $e_{0}^{\prime}$. We define linear operators $x_{0}$ and $x_{1}$ on $V$ by $$  egin{aligned} & x_{0} e_{r}=i e_{r+1} \quad 	ext { for } r 
eq k-1, m+k, \ & x_{0} e_{k-1}=i\left(e_{k}+\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}ight) \quad 	ext { if } k>0, \ & x_{0} e_{m+k}=i \varepsilon e_{m+1}^{\prime} \quad\left(e_{m+1}^{\prime}=0 	ext { if } k=0ight), \ & x_{0} e_{r}^{\prime}=i e_{r+1}^{\prime} \quad(0 \leqslant r<m+k), \quad x_{0} e_{m+k}^{\prime}=0 ; \ & x_{1} e_{r}=0 \quad 	ext { for } r 
eq k, m+k, \ & x_{1} e_{k}=i \varepsilon^{\prime} e_{0}^{\prime}, \quad x_{1} e_{m+k}=i \varepsilon^{\prime} e_{m}^{\prime}, \ & x_{1} e_{r}^{\prime}=0 \quad(0 \leqslant r \leqslant m+k) . \end{aligned} $$ From the definition of $x_{0}$ and from (10.5) it follows that $f\left(x_{0} e_{r}, e_{s}ight)=0=f\left(e_{r}, x_{0} e_{s}ight)$ for all $r, s$ except (when $k>0$ ) that $$  egin{aligned} & f\left(x_{0} e_{k-1}, e_{m+k}ight)=-i \varepsilon=f\left(x_{0} e_{m+k}, e_{k-1}ight), \ & f\left(e_{k-1}, x_{0} e_{m+k}ight)=i \varepsilon=f\left(e_{m+k}, x_{0} e_{k-1}ight) . \end{aligned} $$ Hence for all $r, s$ we have $f\left(x_{0} e_{r}, e_{s}ight)+f\left(e_{r}, x_{0} e_{s}ight)=0$.\ Since the subspace spanned by $e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{m+k}^{\prime}$ is totally isotropic it is clear that $f\left(x_{0} e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)+f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, x_{0} e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0$ holds for all $r, s$. We have $f\left(x_{0} e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0=f\left(e_{r}, x_{0} e_{s}^{\prime}ight)$ for all $r, s$ except that $$  egin{aligned} & f\left(x_{0} e_{r}, e_{m+k-r-1}^{\prime}ight)=i \quad(0 \leqslant r<m+k), \ & f\left(e_{r}, x_{0} e_{m+k-r-1}^{\prime}ight)=-i \quad(0 \leqslant r<m+k) . \end{aligned} $$ Thus for all $r, s$ we have $f\left(x_{0} e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)+f\left(e_{r}, x_{0} e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0$.\ Since $f$ is a hermitian form, it follows that $f\left(x_{0} v_{1}, v_{2}ight)+f\left(v_{1}, x_{0} v_{2}ight)=0$ for all $v_{1}, v_{2} \in V$, i.e., $x_{0} \in L$. It is obvious that $f\left(x_{1} e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)+f\left(e_{r}, x_{1} e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0$ and $f\left(x_{1} e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)+f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, x_{1} e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0$ for all $r, s$. We have $f\left(x_{1} e_{r}, e_{s}ight)=0=f\left(e_{r}, x_{1} e_{s}ight)$ for all $r, s$ except for $$  egin{aligned} & f\left(x_{1} e_{k}, e_{m+k}ight)=-i \varepsilon^{\prime}=f\left(x_{1} e_{m+k}, e_{k}ight), \ & f\left(e_{k}, x_{1} e_{m+k}ight)=i \varepsilon^{\prime}=f\left(e_{m+k}, x_{1} e_{k}ight) . \end{aligned} $$ Hence $f\left(x_{1} e_{r}, e_{s}ight)+f\left(e_{r}, x_{1} e_{s}ight)=0$ for all $r, s$. Therefore $x_{1} \in L$ and $x(t)=x_{0}+t x_{1} \in L$ for all real $t$. We claim that $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$. Let first $k=0$, i.e., $m=n$. For real $\lambda$ let $U_{\lambda}$ be the $x_{0}$-invariant subspace generated by the vector $e_{0}+\lambda e_{0}^{\prime}$. The vectors $e_{r}+\lambda e_{r}^{\prime}$ ( $0 \leqslant r \leqslant m$ ) form a basis of $U_{\lambda}$. Since  egin{equation*} \varepsilon(-i)^{m} f\left(e_{0}+\lambda e_{0}^{\prime}, x_{0}^{m}\left(e_{0}+\lambda e_{0}^{\prime}ight)ight)=2 \varepsilon \lambda, 	ag{10.6} \end{equation*} $U_{\lambda}$ is nondegenerate for $\lambda 
eq 0$. (Indeed, if degenerate then $x_{0}^{m}\left(e_{0}+\lambda e_{0}^{\prime}ight)$ would be in its radical.) Since $e_{0}+e_{0}^{\prime}$ is orthogonal to $e_{r}-e_{r}^{\prime}(0 \leqslant r \leqslant m)$, it follows that $V=U_{1} \oplus U_{-1}$ and $U_{1} \perp U_{-1}$. From (10.6) and (5.3) it follows now that $\left(V, f, x_{0}ight) \in \Delta_{m}^{+}(0)+\Delta_{m}^{-}(0)$, and so $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$. Now let $k>0$. We have then $$  egin{aligned} & x_{0}^{n} e_{0}=i^{k} x_{0}^{n-k}\left(e_{k}+\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}ight)=i^{m+k} x_{0}^{k}\left(e_{m+k}+\varepsilon e_{m}^{\prime}ight)=2 \varepsilon i^{n} e_{m+k}^{\prime}, \ & x_{0}^{n+1} e_{0}=0, \quad x_{0}^{m}\left(e_{k}-\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}ight)=i^{m}\left(e_{m+k}-\varepsilon e_{m}^{\prime}ight), \ & x_{0}^{m+1}\left(e_{k}-\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}ight)=0 . \end{aligned} $$ Let $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$ be the $x_{0}$-invariant subspaces generated by $e_{0}$ and $e=e_{k}-\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}$, respectively. Since $e_{m+k}^{\prime}$ and $e_{k}-\varepsilon e_{0}$ are linearly independent vectors in $\operatorname{Ker} x_{0}$, the above equalities imply that $V=V_{1} \oplus V_{2}, \operatorname{dim} V_{1}=n+1$ and $\operatorname{dim} V_{2}=m+1$. Since the vectors $e_{k+r}-\varepsilon e_{r}^{\prime}(0 \leqslant r \leqslant m)$ form a basis of $V_{2}$ and are orthogonal to $e_{0}$, we have $V_{1} \perp V_{2}$. Since $\varepsilon(-i)^{n} f\left(e_{0}, x_{0}^{n} e_{0}ight)=2=-\varepsilon(-i)^{m} f\left(e, x_{0}^{m} eight)$, it follows from §5 that $\left(V, f, x_{0}ight) \in \Delta_{m}^{-\varepsilon}(0)+\Delta_{n}^{\varepsilon}(0)$. Thus again $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$. For $k>0$ we have $$  egin{aligned} x(t)^{n+1} e_{0} & =i^{k} x(t)^{n-k+1}\left(e_{k}+\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}ight)=i^{k+1} x(t)^{n-k}\left(e_{k+1}+\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{0}^{\prime}+\varepsilon e_{1}^{\prime}ight) \ & =i^{m+k} x(t)^{k+1}\left(e_{m+k}+\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m-1}^{\prime}+\varepsilon e_{m}^{\prime}ight) \ & =2 i^{m+k+1} x(t)^{k}\left(\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m}^{\prime}+\varepsilon e_{m+1}^{\prime}ight)=2 i^{n+1} \varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m+k}^{\prime}, \end{aligned} $$ and for $k=0$ $$ x(t)^{n+1} e_{0}=i x(t)^{n}\left(e_{1}+\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{0}^{\prime}ight)=i^{n} x(t)\left(e_{n}+\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{n-1}^{\prime}ight)=2 i^{n+1} \varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{n}^{\prime} . $$ Thus for all $k$ we have  egin{equation*} x(t)^{n+1} e_{0}=2 i^{n+1} \varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m+k}^{\prime}, \quad x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}=0 . 	ag{10.7} \end{equation*} Writing $a=e_{k+1}-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{0}^{\prime}-\varepsilon e_{1}^{\prime}$, we have  egin{equation*} x(t)^{m-1} a=i^{m-1}\left(e_{m+k}-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m-1}^{\prime}-\varepsilon e_{m}^{\prime}ight), \quad x(t)^{m} a=0 . 	ag{10.8} \end{equation*} Fix $t 
eq 0$ and let $W_{1}$ and $W_{2}$ be $x(t)$-invariant subspaces generated by $e_{0}$ and $a$, respectively. Let first $k>0$. Then the vectors $e_{r+k}-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{r-1}^{\prime}-\varepsilon e_{r}^{\prime}(1 \leqslant r \leqslant m)$ form a basis of $W_{2}$ and are orthogonal to $e_{0}$. From (10.7) and (10.8) we conclude that $V=W_{1} \oplus W_{2}, \operatorname{dim} W_{1}=n+2, \operatorname{dim} W_{2}=m$, and $W_{1} \perp W_{2}$. Now let $k=0$ and let $W_{3}$ be the $x(t)$-invariant subspace generated by the vector $b=e_{1}-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{0}^{\prime}$. Then $x(t)^{m-1} b=i^{m-1}\left(e_{m}-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m-1}^{\prime}ight), x(t)^{m} b=0$. Hence the vectors $e_{r}-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{r-1}^{\prime}$ ( $1 \leqslant r \leqslant m$ ) form a basis of $W_{3}$ and are orthogonal to $e_{0}$. It follows that $V=W_{1} \oplus W_{3}$ and $W_{1} \perp W_{3}$. Since $$  egin{aligned} \varepsilon^{\prime}(-i)^{n+1} f\left(e_{0}, x(t)^{n+1} e_{0}ight) & =2 t, \ -\varepsilon^{\prime}(-i)^{m-1} f\left(a, x(t)^{m-1} aight) & =2 t, \ -\varepsilon^{\prime}(-i)^{m-1} f\left(b, x(t)^{m-1} aight) & =2 t \quad(k=0), \end{aligned} $$ it follows that $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ for $t>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Section 10: the case j=4

nodes.name: Rewrite the primitive Pi-mutations as (10.1)-(10.3)
nodes.statement: 10. The case $j=4$. We have $\Phi_{4}=\Pi$ and the primitive $\Pi$-mutations are defined by (8.1)-(8.3). These mutations can also be written as \begin{gather*} g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(n+1) \rightarrow g^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+2), \quad n-m=2 k+1 ; \tag{10.1}\\ g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+1) \rightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m-1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+3), \quad m \leqslant n ; \tag{10.2}\\ g^{-\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+1) \rightarrow g^{-\varepsilon^{\prime}}(m)+g^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(n+2), \quad n-m=2 k ; \tag{10.3} \end{gather*} where $k(\geqslant 0)$ is an integer and $\varepsilon, \varepsilon^{\prime}= \pm$.\\ Indeed, (8.2) and (10.2) list the same mutations. Mutations (8.1) for $n-m$ even are the same as (10.3) for $\varepsilon^{\prime}=\varepsilon$. Mutations (8.1) for $n-m$ odd are the same as (10.1) for $\varepsilon^{\prime}=-\varepsilon$. Mutations (8.3) for $n-m$ even are the same as (10.3) for $\varepsilon^{\prime}=\varepsilon$. Finally, mutations (8.3) for $n-m$ odd are the same as (10.1) for $\varepsilon^{\prime}=\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the primitive Pi-mutations as (10.1)-(10.3)

nodes.name: Mutation (10.1): explicit family and type computation via (5
nodes.statement:
Assume first that the mutation (9.1) is of the form (10.1). We can choose a basis $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{m}, e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{n}^{\prime}$ of $V$ such that  egin{equation*} f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0, \quad f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}ight)=\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m}, \quad f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=\varepsilon^{\prime} \delta_{r+s, n} 	ag{10.4} \end{equation*} holds for all relevant $r, s$. We define linear maps $x_{0}$ and $x_{1}$ on $V$ by specifying their effect on basis elements: $$  egin{array}{ll} x_{0} e_{r}=i e_{r+1} & (0 \leqslant r<m), \quad x_{0} e_{m}=0, \ x_{0} e_{r}^{\prime}=i e_{r+1}^{\prime} & (0 \leqslant r<n), \quad x_{0} e_{n}^{\prime}=0, \end{array} $$ $$  egin{aligned} & x_{1} e_{r}=0 \quad(0 \leqslant r<m), \quad x_{1} e_{m}=i e_{n-k}^{\prime}, \ & x_{1} e_{r}^{\prime}=0 \quad 	ext { for } r 
eq k, \quad x_{1} e_{k}^{\prime}=i \varepsilon \varepsilon^{\prime} e_{0} . \end{aligned} $$ In view of (5.1) and the definition of $x_{0}$ it is clear that $x_{0} \in 	heta_{1}$. It is easy to check that $x_{1} \in L$ and so $x(t) \in L$ for all real $t$. We have $$  egin{aligned} & x(t)^{k+1} e_{0}^{\prime}=x(t) i^{k} e_{k}^{\prime}=i^{k+1}\left(e_{k+1}^{\prime}+\varepsilon \varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{0}ight), \ & x(t)^{k+m+1} e_{0}^{\prime}=i^{k+m+1}\left(e_{k+m+1}^{\prime}+\varepsilon \varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m}ight)=i^{n-k}\left(e_{n-k}^{\prime}+\varepsilon \varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m}ight), \ & x(t)^{n} e_{0}^{\prime}=i^{n-k} x(t)^{k}\left(e_{n-k}^{\prime}+\varepsilon \varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m}ight)=i^{n}\left(e_{n}^{\prime}+\varepsilon \varepsilon^{\prime} t^{2} e_{n-1}^{\prime}ight), \ & x(t)^{n+1} e_{0}^{\prime}=i^{n+1} \varepsilon \varepsilon^{\prime} t^{2} e_{n}^{\prime}, \quad x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}^{\prime}=0, \ & x(t)^{m-1}\left(e_{1}-t e_{k+1}^{\prime}ight)=i^{m-1}\left(e_{m}-t e_{k+m}^{\prime}ight)=i^{m-1}\left(e_{m}-t e_{n-k-1}^{\prime}ight), \ & x(t)^{m}\left(e_{1}-t e_{k+1}^{\prime}ight)=0 . \end{aligned} $$ We now assume that $t 
eq 0$. Let $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$ be the $x(t)$-invariant subspaces generated by the vectors $e_{0}^{\prime}$ and $e=e_{1}-t e_{k+1}^{\prime}$, respectively. It is clear that $V=V_{1} \oplus V_{2}$, $\operatorname{dim} V_{1}=n+2, \operatorname{dim} V_{2}=m$. Note that the vectors $e_{r}-t e_{r+k}^{\prime}(1 \leqslant r \leqslant m)$ form a basis of $V_{2}$ and are orthogonal to $e_{0}^{\prime}$. Hence $V_{1} \cap V_{2}^{\perp}$ is an $x(t)$-invariant subspace of $V_{1}$ containing $e_{0}^{\prime}$. It follows from the definition of $V_{1}$ that $V_{1} \cap V_{2}^{\perp}=V_{1}$, i.e., $V_{1}=V_{2}^{\perp}$. Let $\Delta_{1}$ and $\Delta_{2}$ be the types which correspond to $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$, respectively. Since $$ \varepsilon(-i)^{n+1} f\left(e_{0}^{\prime}, x(t)^{n+1} e_{0}^{\prime}ight)=t^{2}=\varepsilon^{\prime}(-i)^{m-1} f\left(e, x(t)^{m-1} eight), $$ it follows from (5.3) that $$ \Delta_{1}=\Delta_{n+1}^{\varepsilon}(0), \quad \Delta_{2}=\Delta_{m-1}^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(0) . $$ Hence indeed $\Delta_{1}+\Delta_{2}=\Delta\left(\mathcal{O}_{2}ight)$, and so $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ for $t 
eq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Mutation (10.1): explicit family and type computation via (5.3)

nodes.name: Mutation (10.2): explicit family and type computation
nodes.statement:
Next assume that the mutation (9.1) is of the form (10.2). Then we can choose a basis $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{m}, e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{n}^{\prime}$ of $V$ such that (10.4) holds with $\varepsilon^{\prime}=\varepsilon$. We define $x(t)$ by $$  egin{aligned} & x(t) e_{0}=i\left(e_{1}+t e_{0}^{\prime}ight), \quad x(t) e_{r}=i e_{r+1} \quad(0<r<m), \quad x(t) e_{m}=0, \ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime}=i e_{r+1}^{\prime} \quad(0 \leqslant r<n), \quad x(t) e_{n}^{\prime}=i t e_{m} . \end{aligned} $$ As in the previous case we have $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$ and $x_{1} \in L$. We have $$  egin{aligned} & x(t)^{m} e_{0}=i x(t)^{m-1}\left(e_{1}+t e_{0}^{\prime}ight)=i^{m}\left(e_{m}+t e_{m-1}^{\prime}ight) \ & x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}=i^{m} x(t)^{n-m+2} t e_{m-1}^{\prime}=i^{n+1} t x(t) e_{n}^{\prime}=i^{n+2} t^{2} e_{m}, \ & x(t)^{n+3} e_{0}=0 . \end{aligned} $$ If $m 
eq 1$ we have $$ x(t)^{m-2}\left(t e_{1}-e_{n-m+2}^{\prime}ight)=i^{m-2}\left(t e_{m-1}-e_{n}^{\prime}ight), x(t)^{m-1}\left(t e_{1}-e_{n-m+2}^{\prime}ight)=0 . $$ Let $t 
eq 0$ and let $V_{1}$ be the $x(t)$-invariant subspace generated by $e_{0}$. Clearly, $\operatorname{dim} V_{1}=n+3$ and so if $m=1$ we have $V_{1}=V$. When $m 
eq 1$ let $V_{2}$ be the $x(t)$-invariant subspace generated by the vector $e=t e_{1}-e_{n-m+2}^{\prime}$. Clearly, $\operatorname{dim} V_{2}=m-1$ and $V=V_{1} \oplus V_{2}$. The vectors $t e_{r}-e_{n-m+r+1}^{\prime}(1 \leqslant r \leqslant m-1)$ form a basis of $V_{2}$ and are orthogonal to $e_{0}$. As in the previous case this implies that\ $V_{1}=V_{2}^{\perp}$. Let $\Delta_{1}$ be the type associated with $V_{1}$ and if $m 
eq 1$ let $\Delta_{2}$ be the type associated with $V_{2}$. Since $$ \varepsilon(-i)^{n+2} f\left(e_{0}, x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}ight)=t^{2}, $$ and if $m 
eq 1$ $$ \varepsilon(-i)^{m-2} f\left(e, x(t)^{m-2} eight)=t^{2}, $$ we have $\Delta_{1}=\Delta_{n+2}^{\varepsilon}(0), \Delta_{2}=\Delta_{m-2}^{\varepsilon}(0)(m 
eq 1)$. Thus $\Delta_{1}=\Delta\left(\mathcal{O}_{2}ight)$ if $m=1$ and $\Delta_{1}+\Delta_{2}=\Delta\left(\mathcal{O}_{2}ight)$ if $m 
eq 1$. Therefore $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ for $t 
eq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Mutation (10.2): explicit family and type computation

nodes.name: Mutation (10.3): explicit family
nodes.statement:
Finally assume that the mutation (9.1) is of the form (10.3). Then we can choose a basis $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{m+k}, e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{m+k}^{\prime}$ of $V$ such that  egin{equation*} f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}ight)=f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0, \quad f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=\delta_{r+s, m+k} 	ag{10.5} \end{equation*} holds for all $r, s$. We define linear operators $x_{0}$ and $x_{1}$ on $V$ by $$  egin{aligned} & x_{0} e_{r}=i e_{r+1} \quad 	ext { for } r 
eq k-1, m+k, \ & x_{0} e_{k-1}=i\left(e_{k}+\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}ight) \quad 	ext { if } k>0, \ & x_{0} e_{m+k}=i \varepsilon e_{m+1}^{\prime} \quad\left(e_{m+1}^{\prime}=0 	ext { if } k=0ight), \ & x_{0} e_{r}^{\prime}=i e_{r+1}^{\prime} \quad(0 \leqslant r<m+k), \quad x_{0} e_{m+k}^{\prime}=0 ; \ & x_{1} e_{r}=0 \quad 	ext { for } r 
eq k, m+k, \ & x_{1} e_{k}=i \varepsilon^{\prime} e_{0}^{\prime}, \quad x_{1} e_{m+k}=i \varepsilon^{\prime} e_{m}^{\prime}, \ & x_{1} e_{r}^{\prime}=0 \quad(0 \leqslant r \leqslant m+k) . \end{aligned} $$ From the definition of $x_{0}$ and from (10.5) it follows that $f\left(x_{0} e_{r}, e_{s}ight)=0=f\left(e_{r}, x_{0} e_{s}ight)$ for all $r, s$ except (when $k>0$ ) that $$  egin{aligned} & f\left(x_{0} e_{k-1}, e_{m+k}ight)=-i \varepsilon=f\left(x_{0} e_{m+k}, e_{k-1}ight), \ & f\left(e_{k-1}, x_{0} e_{m+k}ight)=i \varepsilon=f\left(e_{m+k}, x_{0} e_{k-1}ight) . \end{aligned} $$ Hence for all $r, s$ we have $f\left(x_{0} e_{r}, e_{s}ight)+f\left(e_{r}, x_{0} e_{s}ight)=0$.\ Since the subspace spanned by $e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{m+k}^{\prime}$ is totally isotropic it is clear that $f\left(x_{0} e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)+f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, x_{0} e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0$ holds for all $r, s$. We have $f\left(x_{0} e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0=f\left(e_{r}, x_{0} e_{s}^{\prime}ight)$ for all $r, s$ except that $$  egin{aligned} & f\left(x_{0} e_{r}, e_{m+k-r-1}^{\prime}ight)=i \quad(0 \leqslant r<m+k), \ & f\left(e_{r}, x_{0} e_{m+k-r-1}^{\prime}ight)=-i \quad(0 \leqslant r<m+k) . \end{aligned} $$ Thus for all $r, s$ we have $f\left(x_{0} e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)+f\left(e_{r}, x_{0} e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0$.\ Since $f$ is a hermitian form, it follows that $f\left(x_{0} v_{1}, v_{2}ight)+f\left(v_{1}, x_{0} v_{2}ight)=0$ for all $v_{1}, v_{2} \in V$, i.e., $x_{0} \in L$. It is obvious that $f\left(x_{1} e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)+f\left(e_{r}, x_{1} e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0$ and $f\left(x_{1} e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)+f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, x_{1} e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0$ for all $r, s$. We have $f\left(x_{1} e_{r}, e_{s}ight)=0=f\left(e_{r}, x_{1} e_{s}ight)$ for all $r, s$ except for $$  egin{aligned} & f\left(x_{1} e_{k}, e_{m+k}ight)=-i \varepsilon^{\prime}=f\left(x_{1} e_{m+k}, e_{k}ight), \ & f\left(e_{k}, x_{1} e_{m+k}ight)=i \varepsilon^{\prime}=f\left(e_{m+k}, x_{1} e_{k}ight) . \end{aligned} $$ Hence $f\left(x_{1} e_{r}, e_{s}ight)+f\left(e_{r}, x_{1} e_{s}ight)=0$ for all $r, s$. Therefore $x_{1} \in L$ and $x(t)=x_{0}+t x_{1} \in L$ for all real $t$. We claim that $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$. Let first $k=0$, i.e., $m=n$. For real $\lambda$ let $U_{\lambda}$ be the $x_{0}$-invariant subspace generated by the vector $e_{0}+\lambda e_{0}^{\prime}$. The vectors $e_{r}+\lambda e_{r}^{\prime}$ ( $0 \leqslant r \leqslant m$ ) form a basis of $U_{\lambda}$. Since  egin{equation*} \varepsilon(-i)^{m} f\left(e_{0}+\lambda e_{0}^{\prime}, x_{0}^{m}\left(e_{0}+\lambda e_{0}^{\prime}ight)ight)=2 \varepsilon \lambda, 	ag{10.6} \end{equation*} $U_{\lambda}$ is nondegenerate for $\lambda 
eq 0$. (Indeed, if degenerate then $x_{0}^{m}\left(e_{0}+\lambda e_{0}^{\prime}ight)$ would be in its radical.) Since $e_{0}+e_{0}^{\prime}$ is orthogonal to $e_{r}-e_{r}^{\prime}(0 \leqslant r \leqslant m)$, it follows that $V=U_{1} \oplus U_{-1}$ and $U_{1} \perp U_{-1}$. From (10.6) and (5.3) it follows now that $\left(V, f, x_{0}ight) \in \Delta_{m}^{+}(0)+\Delta_{m}^{-}(0)$, and so $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$. Now let $k>0$. We have then $$  egin{aligned} & x_{0}^{n} e_{0}=i^{k} x_{0}^{n-k}\left(e_{k}+\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}ight)=i^{m+k} x_{0}^{k}\left(e_{m+k}+\varepsilon e_{m}^{\prime}ight)=2 \varepsilon i^{n} e_{m+k}^{\prime}, \ & x_{0}^{n+1} e_{0}=0, \quad x_{0}^{m}\left(e_{k}-\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}ight)=i^{m}\left(e_{m+k}-\varepsilon e_{m}^{\prime}ight), \ & x_{0}^{m+1}\left(e_{k}-\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}ight)=0 . \end{aligned} $$ Let $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$ be the $x_{0}$-invariant subspaces generated by $e_{0}$ and $e=e_{k}-\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}$, respectively. Since $e_{m+k}^{\prime}$ and $e_{k}-\varepsilon e_{0}$ are linearly independent vectors in $\operatorname{Ker} x_{0}$, the above equalities imply that $V=V_{1} \oplus V_{2}, \operatorname{dim} V_{1}=n+1$ and $\operatorname{dim} V_{2}=m+1$. Since the vectors $e_{k+r}-\varepsilon e_{r}^{\prime}(0 \leqslant r \leqslant m)$ form a basis of $V_{2}$ and are orthogonal to $e_{0}$, we have $V_{1} \perp V_{2}$. Since $\varepsilon(-i)^{n} f\left(e_{0}, x_{0}^{n} e_{0}ight)=2=-\varepsilon(-i)^{m} f\left(e, x_{0}^{m} eight)$, it follows from §5 that $\left(V, f, x_{0}ight) \in \Delta_{m}^{-\varepsilon}(0)+\Delta_{n}^{\varepsilon}(0)$. Thus again $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$. For $k>0$ we have $$  egin{aligned} x(t)^{n+1} e_{0} & =i^{k} x(t)^{n-k+1}\left(e_{k}+\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}ight)=i^{k+1} x(t)^{n-k}\left(e_{k+1}+\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{0}^{\prime}+\varepsilon e_{1}^{\prime}ight) \ & =i^{m+k} x(t)^{k+1}\left(e_{m+k}+\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m-1}^{\prime}+\varepsilon e_{m}^{\prime}ight) \ & =2 i^{m+k+1} x(t)^{k}\left(\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m}^{\prime}+\varepsilon e_{m+1}^{\prime}ight)=2 i^{n+1} \varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m+k}^{\prime}, \end{aligned} $$ and for $k=0$ $$ x(t)^{n+1} e_{0}=i x(t)^{n}\left(e_{1}+\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{0}^{\prime}ight)=i^{n} x(t)\left(e_{n}+\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{n-1}^{\prime}ight)=2 i^{n+1} \varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{n}^{\prime} . $$ Thus for all $k$ we have  egin{equation*} x(t)^{n+1} e_{0}=2 i^{n+1} \varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m+k}^{\prime}, \quad x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}=0 . 	ag{10.7} \end{equation*} Writing $a=e_{k+1}-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{0}^{\prime}-\varepsilon e_{1}^{\prime}$, we have  egin{equation*} x(t)^{m-1} a=i^{m-1}\left(e_{m+k}-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m-1}^{\prime}-\varepsilon e_{m}^{\prime}ight), \quad x(t)^{m} a=0 . 	ag{10.8} \end{equation*} Fix $t 
eq 0$ and let $W_{1}$ and $W_{2}$ be $x(t)$-invariant subspaces generated by $e_{0}$ and $a$, respectively. Let first $k>0$. Then the vectors $e_{r+k}-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{r-1}^{\prime}-\varepsilon e_{r}^{\prime}(1 \leqslant r \leqslant m)$ form a basis of $W_{2}$ and are orthogonal to $e_{0}$. From (10.7) and (10.8) we conclude that $V=W_{1} \oplus W_{2}, \operatorname{dim} W_{1}=n+2, \operatorname{dim} W_{2}=m$, and $W_{1} \perp W_{2}$. Now let $k=0$ and let $W_{3}$ be the $x(t)$-invariant subspace generated by the vector $b=e_{1}-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{0}^{\prime}$. Then $x(t)^{m-1} b=i^{m-1}\left(e_{m}-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m-1}^{\prime}ight), x(t)^{m} b=0$. Hence the vectors $e_{r}-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{r-1}^{\prime}$ ( $1 \leqslant r \leqslant m$ ) form a basis of $W_{3}$ and are orthogonal to $e_{0}$. It follows that $V=W_{1} \oplus W_{3}$ and $W_{1} \perp W_{3}$. Since $$  egin{aligned} \varepsilon^{\prime}(-i)^{n+1} f\left(e_{0}, x(t)^{n+1} e_{0}ight) & =2 t, \ -\varepsilon^{\prime}(-i)^{m-1} f\left(a, x(t)^{m-1} aight) & =2 t, \ -\varepsilon^{\prime}(-i)^{m-1} f\left(b, x(t)^{m-1} aight) & =2 t \quad(k=0), \end{aligned} $$ it follows that $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ for $t>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Mutation (10.3): explicit family

nodes.name: Choose a basis satisfying (10.5) and define x0, x1
nodes.statement: Finally assume that the mutation (9.1) is of the form (10.3). Then we can choose a basis $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{m+k}, e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{m+k}^{\prime}$ of $V$ such that \begin{equation*} f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}\right)=f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}\right)=0, \quad f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}\right)=\delta_{r+s, m+k} \tag{10.5} \end{equation*} holds for all $r, s$. We define linear operators $x_{0}$ and $x_{1}$ on $V$ by $$ \begin{aligned} & x_{0} e_{r}=i e_{r+1} \quad \text { for } r \neq k-1, m+k, \\ & x_{0} e_{k-1}=i\left(e_{k}+\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}\right) \quad \text { if } k>0, \\ & x_{0} e_{m+k}=i \varepsilon e_{m+1}^{\prime} \quad\left(e_{m+1}^{\prime}=0 \text { if } k=0\right), \\ & x_{0} e_{r}^{\prime}=i e_{r+1}^{\prime} \quad(0 \leqslant r<m+k), \quad x_{0} e_{m+k}^{\prime}=0 ; \\ & x_{1} e_{r}=0 \quad \text { for } r \neq k, m+k, \\ & x_{1} e_{k}=i \varepsilon^{\prime} e_{0}^{\prime}, \quad x_{1} e_{m+k}=i \varepsilon^{\prime} e_{m}^{\prime}, \\ & x_{1} e_{r}^{\prime}=0 \quad(0 \leqslant r \leqslant m+k) . \end{aligned} $$
nodes.statement_short: Choose a basis satisfying (10.5) and define x0, x1

nodes.name: Verify x0, x1 lie in L
nodes.statement: From the definition of $x_{0}$ and from (10.5) it follows that $f\left(x_{0} e_{r}, e_{s}\right)=0=f\left(e_{r}, x_{0} e_{s}\right)$ for all $r, s$ except (when $k>0$ ) that $$ \begin{aligned} & f\left(x_{0} e_{k-1}, e_{m+k}\right)=-i \varepsilon=f\left(x_{0} e_{m+k}, e_{k-1}\right), \\ & f\left(e_{k-1}, x_{0} e_{m+k}\right)=i \varepsilon=f\left(e_{m+k}, x_{0} e_{k-1}\right) . \end{aligned} $$ Hence for all $r, s$ we have $f\left(x_{0} e_{r}, e_{s}\right)+f\left(e_{r}, x_{0} e_{s}\right)=0$.\\ Since the subspace spanned by $e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{m+k}^{\prime}$ is totally isotropic it is clear that $f\left(x_{0} e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}\right)+f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, x_{0} e_{s}^{\prime}\right)=0$ holds for all $r, s$. We have $f\left(x_{0} e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}\right)=0=f\left(e_{r}, x_{0} e_{s}^{\prime}\right)$ for all $r, s$ except that $$ \begin{aligned} & f\left(x_{0} e_{r}, e_{m+k-r-1}^{\prime}\right)=i \quad(0 \leqslant r<m+k), \\ & f\left(e_{r}, x_{0} e_{m+k-r-1}^{\prime}\right)=-i \quad(0 \leqslant r<m+k) . \end{aligned} $$ Thus for all $r, s$ we have $f\left(x_{0} e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}\right)+f\left(e_{r}, x_{0} e_{s}^{\prime}\right)=0$.\\ Since $f$ is a hermitian form, it follows that $f\left(x_{0} v_{1}, v_{2}\right)+f\left(v_{1}, x_{0} v_{2}\right)=0$ for all $v_{1}, v_{2} \in V$, i.e., $x_{0} \in L$. It is obvious that $f\left(x_{1} e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}\right)+f\left(e_{r}, x_{1} e_{s}^{\prime}\right)=0$ and $f\left(x_{1} e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}\right)+f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, x_{1} e_{s}^{\prime}\right)=0$ for all $r, s$. We have $f\left(x_{1} e_{r}, e_{s}\right)=0=f\left(e_{r}, x_{1} e_{s}\right)$ for all $r, s$ except for $$ \begin{aligned} & f\left(x_{1} e_{k}, e_{m+k}\right)=-i \varepsilon^{\prime}=f\left(x_{1} e_{m+k}, e_{k}\right), \\ & f\left(e_{k}, x_{1} e_{m+k}\right)=i \varepsilon^{\prime}=f\left(e_{m+k}, x_{1} e_{k}\right) . \end{aligned} $$ Hence $f\left(x_{1} e_{r}, e_{s}\right)+f\left(e_{r}, x_{1} e_{s}\right)=0$ for all $r, s$. Therefore $x_{1} \in L$ and $x(t)=x_{0}+t x_{1} \in L$ for all real $t$.
nodes.statement_short: Verify x0, x1 lie in L

nodes.name: Claim: x0 lies in O1
nodes.statement: We claim that $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$. Let first $k=0$, i.e., $m=n$. For real $\lambda$ let $U_{\lambda}$ be the $x_{0}$-invariant subspace generated by the vector $e_{0}+\lambda e_{0}^{\prime}$. The vectors $e_{r}+\lambda e_{r}^{\prime}$ ( $0 \leqslant r \leqslant m$ ) form a basis of $U_{\lambda}$. Since \begin{equation*} \varepsilon(-i)^{m} f\left(e_{0}+\lambda e_{0}^{\prime}, x_{0}^{m}\left(e_{0}+\lambda e_{0}^{\prime}\right)\right)=2 \varepsilon \lambda, \tag{10.6} \end{equation*} $U_{\lambda}$ is nondegenerate for $\lambda \neq 0$. (Indeed, if degenerate then $x_{0}^{m}\left(e_{0}+\lambda e_{0}^{\prime}\right)$ would be in its radical.) Since $e_{0}+e_{0}^{\prime}$ is orthogonal to $e_{r}-e_{r}^{\prime}(0 \leqslant r \leqslant m)$, it follows that $V=U_{1} \oplus U_{-1}$ and $U_{1} \perp U_{-1}$. From (10.6) and (5.3) it follows now that $\left(V, f, x_{0}\right) \in \Delta_{m}^{+}(0)+\Delta_{m}^{-}(0)$, and so $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$. Now let $k>0$. We have then $$ \begin{aligned} & x_{0}^{n} e_{0}=i^{k} x_{0}^{n-k}\left(e_{k}+\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}\right)=i^{m+k} x_{0}^{k}\left(e_{m+k}+\varepsilon e_{m}^{\prime}\right)=2 \varepsilon i^{n} e_{m+k}^{\prime}, \\ & x_{0}^{n+1} e_{0}=0, \quad x_{0}^{m}\left(e_{k}-\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}\right)=i^{m}\left(e_{m+k}-\varepsilon e_{m}^{\prime}\right), \\ & x_{0}^{m+1}\left(e_{k}-\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}\right)=0 . \end{aligned} $$ Let $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$ be the $x_{0}$-invariant subspaces generated by $e_{0}$ and $e=e_{k}-\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}$, respectively. Since $e_{m+k}^{\prime}$ and $e_{k}-\varepsilon e_{0}$ are linearly independent vectors in $\operatorname{Ker} x_{0}$, the above equalities imply that $V=V_{1} \oplus V_{2}, \operatorname{dim} V_{1}=n+1$ and $\operatorname{dim} V_{2}=m+1$. Since the vectors $e_{k+r}-\varepsilon e_{r}^{\prime}(0 \leqslant r \leqslant m)$ form a basis of $V_{2}$ and are orthogonal to $e_{0}$, we have $V_{1} \perp V_{2}$. Since $\varepsilon(-i)^{n} f\left(e_{0}, x_{0}^{n} e_{0}\right)=2=-\varepsilon(-i)^{m} f\left(e, x_{0}^{m} e\right)$, it follows from §5 that $\left(V, f, x_{0}\right) \in \Delta_{m}^{-\varepsilon}(0)+\Delta_{n}^{\varepsilon}(0)$. Thus again $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: x0 lies in O1

nodes.name: Case k=0: split V = U_1 + U_{-1}
nodes.statement: Let first $k=0$, i.e., $m=n$. For real $\lambda$ let $U_{\lambda}$ be the $x_{0}$-invariant subspace generated by the vector $e_{0}+\lambda e_{0}^{\prime}$. The vectors $e_{r}+\lambda e_{r}^{\prime}$ ( $0 \leqslant r \leqslant m$ ) form a basis of $U_{\lambda}$. Since \begin{equation*} \varepsilon(-i)^{m} f\left(e_{0}+\lambda e_{0}^{\prime}, x_{0}^{m}\left(e_{0}+\lambda e_{0}^{\prime}\right)\right)=2 \varepsilon \lambda, \tag{10.6} \end{equation*} $U_{\lambda}$ is nondegenerate for $\lambda \neq 0$. (Indeed, if degenerate then $x_{0}^{m}\left(e_{0}+\lambda e_{0}^{\prime}\right)$ would be in its radical.) Since $e_{0}+e_{0}^{\prime}$ is orthogonal to $e_{r}-e_{r}^{\prime}(0 \leqslant r \leqslant m)$, it follows that $V=U_{1} \oplus U_{-1}$ and $U_{1} \perp U_{-1}$. From (10.6) and (5.3) it follows now that $\left(V, f, x_{0}\right) \in \Delta_{m}^{+}(0)+\Delta_{m}^{-}(0)$, and so $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Case k=0: split V = U_1 + U_{-1}

nodes.name: Case k>0: two orthogonal Jordan blocks
nodes.statement: Now let $k>0$. We have then $$ \begin{aligned} & x_{0}^{n} e_{0}=i^{k} x_{0}^{n-k}\left(e_{k}+\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}\right)=i^{m+k} x_{0}^{k}\left(e_{m+k}+\varepsilon e_{m}^{\prime}\right)=2 \varepsilon i^{n} e_{m+k}^{\prime}, \\ & x_{0}^{n+1} e_{0}=0, \quad x_{0}^{m}\left(e_{k}-\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}\right)=i^{m}\left(e_{m+k}-\varepsilon e_{m}^{\prime}\right), \\ & x_{0}^{m+1}\left(e_{k}-\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}\right)=0 . \end{aligned} $$ Let $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$ be the $x_{0}$-invariant subspaces generated by $e_{0}$ and $e=e_{k}-\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}$, respectively. Since $e_{m+k}^{\prime}$ and $e_{k}-\varepsilon e_{0}$ are linearly independent vectors in $\operatorname{Ker} x_{0}$, the above equalities imply that $V=V_{1} \oplus V_{2}, \operatorname{dim} V_{1}=n+1$ and $\operatorname{dim} V_{2}=m+1$. Since the vectors $e_{k+r}-\varepsilon e_{r}^{\prime}(0 \leqslant r \leqslant m)$ form a basis of $V_{2}$ and are orthogonal to $e_{0}$, we have $V_{1} \perp V_{2}$. Since $\varepsilon(-i)^{n} f\left(e_{0}, x_{0}^{n} e_{0}\right)=2=-\varepsilon(-i)^{m} f\left(e, x_{0}^{m} e\right)$, it follows from §5 that $\left(V, f, x_{0}\right) \in \Delta_{m}^{-\varepsilon}(0)+\Delta_{n}^{\varepsilon}(0)$. Thus again $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Case k>0: two orthogonal Jordan blocks

nodes.name: Compute x(t) powers and conclude x(t) in O2
nodes.statement: For $k>0$ we have $$ \begin{aligned} x(t)^{n+1} e_{0} & =i^{k} x(t)^{n-k+1}\left(e_{k}+\varepsilon e_{0}^{\prime}\right)=i^{k+1} x(t)^{n-k}\left(e_{k+1}+\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{0}^{\prime}+\varepsilon e_{1}^{\prime}\right) \\ & =i^{m+k} x(t)^{k+1}\left(e_{m+k}+\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m-1}^{\prime}+\varepsilon e_{m}^{\prime}\right) \\ & =2 i^{m+k+1} x(t)^{k}\left(\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m}^{\prime}+\varepsilon e_{m+1}^{\prime}\right)=2 i^{n+1} \varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m+k}^{\prime}, \end{aligned} $$ and for $k=0$ $$ x(t)^{n+1} e_{0}=i x(t)^{n}\left(e_{1}+\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{0}^{\prime}\right)=i^{n} x(t)\left(e_{n}+\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{n-1}^{\prime}\right)=2 i^{n+1} \varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{n}^{\prime} . $$ Thus for all $k$ we have \begin{equation*} x(t)^{n+1} e_{0}=2 i^{n+1} \varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m+k}^{\prime}, \quad x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}=0 . \tag{10.7} \end{equation*} Writing $a=e_{k+1}-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{0}^{\prime}-\varepsilon e_{1}^{\prime}$, we have \begin{equation*} x(t)^{m-1} a=i^{m-1}\left(e_{m+k}-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m-1}^{\prime}-\varepsilon e_{m}^{\prime}\right), \quad x(t)^{m} a=0 . \tag{10.8} \end{equation*} Fix $t \neq 0$ and let $W_{1}$ and $W_{2}$ be $x(t)$-invariant subspaces generated by $e_{0}$ and $a$, respectively. Let first $k>0$. Then the vectors $e_{r+k}-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{r-1}^{\prime}-\varepsilon e_{r}^{\prime}(1 \leqslant r \leqslant m)$ form a basis of $W_{2}$ and are orthogonal to $e_{0}$. From (10.7) and (10.8) we conclude that $V=W_{1} \oplus W_{2}, \operatorname{dim} W_{1}=n+2, \operatorname{dim} W_{2}=m$, and $W_{1} \perp W_{2}$. Now let $k=0$ and let $W_{3}$ be the $x(t)$-invariant subspace generated by the vector $b=e_{1}-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{0}^{\prime}$. Then $x(t)^{m-1} b=i^{m-1}\left(e_{m}-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m-1}^{\prime}\right), x(t)^{m} b=0$. Hence the vectors $e_{r}-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{r-1}^{\prime}$ ( $1 \leqslant r \leqslant m$ ) form a basis of $W_{3}$ and are orthogonal to $e_{0}$. It follows that $V=W_{1} \oplus W_{3}$ and $W_{1} \perp W_{3}$. Since $$ \begin{aligned} \varepsilon^{\prime}(-i)^{n+1} f\left(e_{0}, x(t)^{n+1} e_{0}\right) & =2 t, \\ -\varepsilon^{\prime}(-i)^{m-1} f\left(a, x(t)^{m-1} a\right) & =2 t, \\ -\varepsilon^{\prime}(-i)^{m-1} f\left(b, x(t)^{m-1} a\right) & =2 t \quad(k=0), \end{aligned} $$ it follows that $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ for $t>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute x(t) powers and conclude x(t) in O2

nodes.name: Section 11: reduce j=7,10 to j=4
nodes.statement: 11. The cases $j=7,10$. We shall reduce these cases to the previous case $j=4$. Recall that $\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{7}=(\Pi, \Lambda)$ and $\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{10}=(\Lambda, \Pi)$. Given $X \in \Pi$ we shall denote by $\sigma(X)$, resp. $\tau(X)$, the chromosome in $(\Pi, \Lambda)$, resp. ( $\Lambda, \Pi$ ), which is obtained from $X$ by ignoring the polarization of its odd, resp. even, genes. Clearly $\sigma: \Pi \rightarrow(\Pi, \Lambda)$ and $\tau: \Pi \rightarrow(\Lambda, \Pi)$ are morphisms of monoids. Lemma 7. Every primitive $(\Pi, \Lambda)$-mutation, resp. $(\Lambda, \Pi)$-mutation, is of the form $\sigma(X) \rightarrow \sigma(Y)$, resp. $\tau(X) \rightarrow \tau(Y)$, for a suitable primitive $\Pi$-mutation $X \rightarrow Y$. Proof. We have to show that each of the mutations (8.4)-(8.8) can be obtained by applying $\sigma$ or $\tau$ to a primitive $\Pi$-mutation $X \rightarrow Y$. In the case (8.4) we take $X=g^{-\varepsilon}(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n), \quad Y$ is determined by (8.4). In the case (8.5) we take $X=g^{-\varepsilon}(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n), \quad Y=g^{\varepsilon}(m-1)+g^{-\varepsilon}(n+1)$. In the case (8.6) we take $X=g^{\varepsilon}(m)+g^{-\varepsilon}(n), \quad Y=g^{-\varepsilon}(m-1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+1)$. In the case (8.7) we take $Y=g^{-\varepsilon}(m-1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+1), X$ being already determined by (8.7). The mutations (8.8) are also primitive $\Pi$-mutations. Let $U$ be a classical group of the fourth series defined by a pair $(W, g)$. Let $W^{\prime}=W \otimes_{\mathbf{C}} \mathbf{H}$ and let $g_{\sigma}$, resp. $g_{\tau}$, be the skew-hermitian, resp. hermitian, form on $W^{\prime}$ whose restriction to $W$ is -ig, resp. $g$. Since $g$ is nondegenerate, so are $g_{\sigma}$ and $g_{\tau}$. Let $U_{\sigma}$, resp. $U_{\tau}$, be the classical group of the seventh, resp. tenth, series defined by the pair $\left(W^{\prime}, g_{\sigma}\right)$, resp. $\left(W^{\prime}, g_{\tau}\right)$. Clearly we may view $U$ as a subgroup of $U_{\sigma}$ and $U_{\tau}$. Let $M$ (resp. $M_{\sigma}, M_{\tau}$ ) be the Lie algebra of $U$ (resp. $U_{\sigma}, U_{\tau}$ ). We shall view $M$ as a subalgebra of $M_{\sigma}$ and $M_{\tau}$. Let $x \in M$ be a nilpotent element, $\Delta$ the type determined by $(W, g, x)$ and $X=X(\Delta) \in \Pi$ the corresponding chromosome. Similarly, let $\Delta_{\sigma}$, resp. $\Delta_{\tau}$, be the type determined by ( $W^{\prime}, g_{\sigma}, x$ ), resp. ( $W^{\prime}, g_{\tau}, x$ ), and let $X_{\sigma}$, resp. $X_{\tau}$, be its chromosome in $(\Pi, \Lambda)$, resp. $(\Lambda, \Pi)$. Lemma 8. With the above notation we have $X_{\sigma}=\sigma(X)$ and $X_{\tau}=\tau(X)$.\\ Proof. It suffices to prove this when $\Delta$ is indecomposable, i.e., $X$ is a gene, say $X=g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)$. We may assume (see §5) that there is a basis $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{m}$ of $W$ such that \begin{equation*} g\left(e_{r}, e_{s}\right)=\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m} \tag{11.1} \end{equation*} for all $r, s$ and \begin{equation*} x e_{r}=e_{r+1} i \quad(0 \leqslant r<m), \quad x e_{m}=0 . \tag{11.2} \end{equation*} Since $W^{\prime}$ is indecomposable with respect to $x$, we must have $X_{\sigma}=g(m+1)$ for $m$ even and $X_{\tau}=g(m+1)$ for $m$ odd. If $m$ is odd we have $i^{m-1} \varepsilon g_{\sigma}\left(e_{0}, x^{m} e_{0}\right)=$ $-i^{m} \varepsilon g\left(e_{0}, e_{m} i^{m}\right)=1$ by (11.1), (11.2) and the definition of $g_{\sigma}$. By (5.5) we have\\ $X_{\sigma}=g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)$ in this case. If $m$ is even then $i^{m} \varepsilon g_{\tau}\left(e_{0}, x^{m} e_{0}\right)=i^{m} \varepsilon g\left(e_{0}, e_{m} i^{m}\right)=1$, and so by (5.4) we have $X_{\tau}=g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)$. Thus $X_{\sigma}=\sigma(X)$ and $X_{\tau}=\tau(X)$ in all cases.\\ We now proceed with our proof of the sufficiency part of Theorem 5. We shall consider in detail the case $j=7$. Then, by hypothesis, (9.1) is a primitive $(\Pi, \Lambda)$-mutation. By Lemma 7 there exists a primitive $\Pi$-mutation $Y_{1} \rightarrow Y_{2}$ such that $\sigma\left(Y_{r}\right)=X_{r}(r=1,2)$. From §5 it is easy to deduce that there exists a C-subspace $V_{0}$ of $V$ such that the canonical map $V_{0} \otimes_{\mathbf{C}} \mathbf{H} \rightarrow V$ is an isomorphism, $f$ takes complex values on $V_{0} \times V_{0}$, and $\operatorname{sig}\left(i f_{0}\right)=\operatorname{sig} Y_{1}=\operatorname{sig} Y_{2}$ where $f_{0}$ is the restriction of $f$ to $V_{0}$. Let $U$ be the classical group of the fourth series defined by the pair $\left(V_{0}, i f_{0}\right)$. Then we have $U_{\sigma}=G$. Let $\mathcal{O}_{r}^{\prime}(r=1,2)$ be the nilpotent orbit of $U$ in its Lie algebra $M$ with the associated chromosome $Y_{r}$. If we identify $M_{\sigma}$ with $L$, then Lemma 8 implies that $\mathcal{O}_{r}^{\prime} \subset \mathcal{O}_{r}(r=1,2)$. Since $Y_{1} \leqslant Y_{2}$, we have $\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime} \leqslant \mathcal{O}_{2}^{\prime}$ by the case $j=4$. This clearly implies that $\mathcal{O}_{1} \leqslant \mathcal{O}_{2}$. The proof in the case $j=10$ is similar and we may safely omit the details.
nodes.statement_short: Section 11: reduce j=7,10 to j=4

nodes.name: Lemma 7 and its proof
nodes.statement: Lemma 7. Every primitive $(\Pi, \Lambda)$-mutation, resp. $(\Lambda, \Pi)$-mutation, is of the form $\sigma(X) \rightarrow \sigma(Y)$, resp. $\tau(X) \rightarrow \tau(Y)$, for a suitable primitive $\Pi$-mutation $X \rightarrow Y$. nodes.name: Reduce to checking (8.4)-(8.8)

nodes.name: Case (8.4)
nodes.statement: In the case (8.4) we take $X=g^{-\varepsilon}(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n), \quad Y$ is determined by (8.4).

nodes.name: Case (8.5)

nodes.name: Quaternionic extension of a U(p,q) and its Lie algebra
nodes.statement: Let $U$ be a classical group of the fourth series defined by a pair $(W, g)$. Let $W^{\prime}=W \otimes_{\mathbf{C}} \mathbf{H}$ and let $g_{\sigma}$, resp. $g_{\tau}$, be the skew-hermitian, resp. hermitian, form on $W^{\prime}$ whose restriction to $W$ is -ig, resp. $g$. Since $g$ is nondegenerate, so are $g_{\sigma}$ and $g_{\tau}$. Let $U_{\sigma}$, resp. $U_{\tau}$, be the classical group of the seventh, resp. tenth, series defined by the pair $\left(W^{\prime}, g_{\sigma}\right)$, resp. $\left(W^{\prime}, g_{\tau}\right)$. Clearly we may view $U$ as a subgroup of $U_{\sigma}$ and $U_{\tau}$. Let $M$ (resp. $M_{\sigma}, M_{\tau}$ ) be the Lie algebra of $U$ (resp. $U_{\sigma}, U_{\tau}$ ). We shall view $M$ as a subalgebra of $M_{\sigma}$ and $M_{\tau}$. Let $x \in M$ be a nilpotent element, $\Delta$ the type determined by $(W, g, x)$ and $X=X(\Delta) \in \Pi$ the corresponding chromosome. Similarly, let $\Delta_{\sigma}$, resp. $\Delta_{\tau}$, be the type determined by ( $W^{\prime}, g_{\sigma}, x$ ), resp. ( $W^{\prime}, g_{\tau}, x$ ), and let $X_{\sigma}$, resp. $X_{\tau}$, be its chromosome in $(\Pi, \Lambda)$, resp. $(\Lambda, \Pi)$.
nodes.statement_short: Quaternionic extension of a U(p,q) and its Lie algebra

nodes.name: Lemma 8 and its proof
nodes.statement: Lemma 8. With the above notation we have $X_{\sigma}=\sigma(X)$ and $X_{\tau}=\tau(X)$.\\ Proof. It suffices to prove this when $\Delta$ is indecomposable, i.e., $X$ is a gene, say $X=g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)$. We may assume (see §5) that there is a basis $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{m}$ of $W$ such that \begin{equation*} g\left(e_{r}, e_{s}\right)=\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m} \tag{11.1} \end{equation*} for all $r, s$ and \begin{equation*} x e_{r}=e_{r+1} i \quad(0 \leqslant r<m), \quad x e_{m}=0 . \tag{11.2} \end{equation*} Since $W^{\prime}$ is indecomposable with respect to $x$, we must have $X_{\sigma}=g(m+1)$ for $m$ even and $X_{\tau}=g(m+1)$ for $m$ odd. If $m$ is odd we have $i^{m-1} \varepsilon g_{\sigma}\left(e_{0}, x^{m} e_{0}\right)=$ $-i^{m} \varepsilon g\left(e_{0}, e_{m} i^{m}\right)=1$ by (11.1), (11.2) and the definition of $g_{\sigma}$. By (5.5) we have\\ $X_{\sigma}=g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)$ in this case. If $m$ is even then $i^{m} \varepsilon g_{\tau}\left(e_{0}, x^{m} e_{0}\right)=i^{m} \varepsilon g\left(e_{0}, e_{m} i^{m}\right)=1$, and so by (5.4) we have $X_{\tau}=g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)$. Thus $X_{\sigma}=\sigma(X)$ and $X_{\tau}=\tau(X)$ in all cases.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 8 and its proof

nodes.statement: If $m$ is odd we have $i^{m-1} \varepsilon g_{\sigma}\left(e_{0}, x^{m} e_{0}\right)=$ $-i^{m} \varepsilon g\left(e_{0}, e_{m} i^{m}\right)=1$ by (11.1), (11.2) and the definition of $g_{\sigma}$. By (5.5) we have\\ $X_{\sigma}=g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)$ in this case.

nodes.statement: Thus $X_{\sigma}=\sigma(X)$ and $X_{\tau}=\tau(X)$ in all cases.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude

nodes.name: Lift the mutation by Lemma 7, embed U into G and apply the c
nodes.statement: We now proceed with our proof of the sufficiency part of Theorem 5. We shall consider in detail the case $j=7$. Then, by hypothesis, (9.1) is a primitive $(\Pi, \Lambda)$-mutation. By Lemma 7 there exists a primitive $\Pi$-mutation $Y_{1} \rightarrow Y_{2}$ such that $\sigma\left(Y_{r}\right)=X_{r}(r=1,2)$. From §5 it is easy to deduce that there exists a C-subspace $V_{0}$ of $V$ such that the canonical map $V_{0} \otimes_{\mathbf{C}} \mathbf{H} \rightarrow V$ is an isomorphism, $f$ takes complex values on $V_{0} \times V_{0}$, and $\operatorname{sig}\left(i f_{0}\right)=\operatorname{sig} Y_{1}=\operatorname{sig} Y_{2}$ where $f_{0}$ is the restriction of $f$ to $V_{0}$. Let $U$ be the classical group of the fourth series defined by the pair $\left(V_{0}, i f_{0}\right)$. Then we have $U_{\sigma}=G$. Let $\mathcal{O}_{r}^{\prime}(r=1,2)$ be the nilpotent orbit of $U$ in its Lie algebra $M$ with the associated chromosome $Y_{r}$. If we identify $M_{\sigma}$ with $L$, then Lemma 8 implies that $\mathcal{O}_{r}^{\prime} \subset \mathcal{O}_{r}(r=1,2)$. Since $Y_{1} \leqslant Y_{2}$, we have $\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime} \leqslant \mathcal{O}_{2}^{\prime}$ by the case $j=4$. This clearly implies that $\mathcal{O}_{1} \leqslant \mathcal{O}_{2}$. The proof in the case $j=10$ is similar and we may safely omit the details.
nodes.statement_short: Lift the mutation by Lemma 7, embed U into G and apply the case j=4 via Lemma 8

nodes.name: Section 12: the cases j=6,9
nodes.statement:
12. The cases $j=6,9$. These two cases will be treated simultaneously. Recall that $\Phi_{6}=(2 \Lambda, \Pi)$ and $\Phi_{9}=(\Pi, 2 \Lambda)$. If $m(\geqslant 0)$ is an integer we shall write $m^{\prime}=\left[ rac{1}{2}(m+1)ight]$. Thus $m=2 m^{\prime}$ for $m$ even and $m=2 m^{\prime}-1$ for $m$ odd. We have  egin{equation*} (-1)^{m-m^{\prime}}=  egin{cases}i^{m} & 	ext { if } m 	ext { is even, } \ i^{m-1} & 	ext { if } m 	ext { is odd. }\end{cases} 	ag{12.1} \end{equation*} Assume first that the mutation (9.1) has the form  egin{equation*} 2 g(m+1) ightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m)+g^{-\varepsilon}(m+2) 	ext {. } 	ag{12.2} \end{equation*} We can choose a basis $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{m}, e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{m}^{\prime}$ of $V$ such that $f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}ight)=f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0$ and $f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=\delta_{r+s, m}$ for all $r, s$. We define the one-parameter family $x(t)=x_{0}+t x_{1}$ of operators in $V$ by $$  egin{aligned} & x(t) e_{0}=e_{1}-\varepsilon(-1)^{m+m^{\prime}} t e_{0}^{\prime} \quad 	ext { if } m>0 \ & x(t) e_{r}=e_{r+1} \quad(0<r<m), \quad x(t) e_{m}=-\varepsilon(-1)^{m^{\prime}} t e_{m}^{\prime}, \ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime}=-e_{r+1}^{\prime} \quad(0 \leqslant r<m), \quad x(t) e_{m}^{\prime}=0 . \end{aligned} $$ It is easy to verify that $x(t) \in L$ for all real $t$. Since $x_{0}$ consists of two Jordan blocks of size $m+1$ each, we have $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$. (Note that $m$ is odd if $j=6$ and $m$ is even if $j=9$.) We have  egin{equation*} x(t)^{m+1} e_{0}=-2 \varepsilon(-1)^{m^{\prime}} t e_{m}^{\prime} \quad 	ext { and } \quad-\varepsilon i^{2 m^{\prime}} f\left(e_{0}, x(t)^{m+1} e_{0}ight)=2 t . 	ag{12.3} \end{equation*} Now let $t>0$. If $m=0$ then $x(t)$ is a single Jordan block and by (5.4)-(5.5) we have $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$. Now let $m \geqslant 1$. Then $x(t)^{m+2}=0$ and $\operatorname{dim} \operatorname{Ker} x(t)=2$. It follows that $x(t)$ consists of two Jordan blocks whose sizes are $m+2$ and $m$. The larger block is the type $\Delta_{m+1}^{-\varepsilon}(0)$ because of (12.3). To avoid tedious computations which are needed to determine the type of the smaller block, we shall use the following ad\ hoc argument. The smaller block is either of type $\Delta_{m-1}^{\varepsilon}(0)$ or of type $\Delta_{m-1}^{-\varepsilon}(0)$. When we let $t ightarrow 0(t>0)$ the type must become $\Delta_{m-1}^{\varepsilon}(0)$. Otherwise there is a strictly decreasing sequence $t_{1}, t_{2}, \ldots$ with limit 0 for which the smaller block is of type $\Delta_{m-1}^{-\varepsilon}(0)$. By the necessity part of Theorem 5, we then obtain $2 g(m+1) \leqslant$ $g^{-\varepsilon}(m+2)+g^{-\varepsilon}(m)$. By applying the priming operation $m-1$ times (see §6) we obtain $2 g(2) \leqslant g^{-\varepsilon}(3)+g^{-\varepsilon}(1)$, which is false. Hence for small positive $t$ the smaller block is of type $\Delta_{m-1}^{\varepsilon}(0)$. Consequently for small positive $t$ we have $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$. Since the set of all $t$ for which the smaller block is of type $\Delta_{m-1}^{\varepsilon}(0)$ (or $\Delta_{m-1}^{-\varepsilon}(0)$ ) is open, it follows that in fact $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ for all $t>0$. Next assume that (9.1) has the form  egin{equation*} g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(n+1) ightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m-1)+g^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(n+3), \quad m \leqslant n . 	ag{12.4} \end{equation*} We can choose a basis $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{m}, e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{n}^{\prime}$ of $V$ such that $f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0$ for all $r, s$ and $f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}ight)=\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m}$ and $f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=\varepsilon^{\prime} \delta_{r+s, n}$ for $r \leqslant s$. The family $x(t)$ is defined by $$  egin{aligned} & x(t) e_{0}=e_{1}+\varepsilon t e_{0}^{\prime}, \ & x(t) e_{r}=e_{r+1} \quad\left(0<r<m^{\prime}ight), \ & x(t) e_{r}=-e_{r+1} \quad\left(m^{\prime} \leqslant r<might), \ & x(t) e_{m}=0, \ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime}=e_{r+1}^{\prime} \quad\left(0 \leqslant r<n^{\prime}ight), \ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime}=-e_{r+1}^{\prime} \quad\left(n^{\prime} \leqslant r<night), \ & x(t) e_{n}^{\prime}=-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m} . \end{aligned} $$ One can easily verify that $x_{0}$ and $x_{1}$ are in $L$ and so $x(t) \in L$ for all real $t$. Moreover it is clear that $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$ (see §5). We have  egin{align*} & x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}=-\varepsilon \varepsilon^{\prime}(-1)^{n-n^{\prime}} t^{2} e_{m}, \quad 	ext { and } \ & \varepsilon^{\prime}(-1)^{n-n^{\prime}+1} f\left(e_{0}, x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}ight)=t^{2} . 	ag{12.5} \end{align*} Now let $t>0$. If $m=1$ then $x(t)$ is a single Jordan block and (12.5) and (5.4)-(5.5) show that it is of type $\Delta_{n+2}^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(0)$. Thus $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ in this case. Now let $m \geqslant 2$. Since $x(t)^{n+3}=0$ and $\operatorname{dim} \operatorname{Ker} x(t)=2, x(t)$ consists of two Jordan blocks whose sizes are $n+3$ and $m-1$. The larger block is of type $\Delta_{n+2}^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(0)$, by (12.5) and (5.4)-(5.5). As in the case (12.2) we can conclude that for $t>0$ the other Jordan block of $x(t)$ must belong to the type $\Delta_{m-2}^{\varepsilon}(0)$. Thus $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ for $t>0$. Now assume that the mutation (9.1) has the form  egin{align*} g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{+}(n & +1)+g^{-}(n+1) \ & ightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m-1)+2 g(n+2), \quad m \leqslant n . 	ag{12.6} \end{align*} We can choose a basis $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{n}, e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{n}^{\prime}, e_{0}^{\prime \prime}, \ldots, e_{m}^{\prime \prime}$ of $V$ such that $f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}ight)=f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0, f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime \prime}ight)=f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime \prime}ight)=0, f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=\delta_{r+s, n}$ for all $r, s$ and $f\left(e_{r}^{\prime \prime}, e_{s}^{\prime \prime}ight)=\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m}$ for $r \leqslant s$. The family $x(t)$ of operators in $V$ is defined by $$  egin{aligned} & x(t) e_{r}=e_{r+1} \quad(0 \leqslant r<n), \quad x(t) e_{n}=0 \ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime}=-e_{r+1}^{\prime} \quad(0 \leqslant r<n), \quad x(t) e_{n}^{\prime}=-\varepsilon t e_{m}^{\prime \prime}, \end{aligned} $$ $$  egin{aligned} & x(t) e_{0}^{\prime \prime}=e_{1}^{\prime \prime}+t e_{0}, \ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime \prime}=e_{r+1}^{\prime \prime} \quad\left(0<r<m^{\prime}ight), \ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime \prime}=-e_{r+1}^{\prime \prime} \quad\left(m^{\prime} \leqslant r<might), \quad x(t) e_{m}^{\prime \prime}=0 . \end{aligned} $$ One can check that $x(t) \in L$ for all real $t$. Let $W, W^{\prime}$ and $W^{\prime \prime}$ be the subspaces of $V$ spanned by the vectors $e_{r}, e_{r}^{\prime}$ and $e_{r}^{\prime \prime}$, respectively. These subspaces are invariant under $x_{0}=x(0)$ and $W^{\prime \prime} \perp\left(W+W^{\prime}ight)$. The restriction of $x_{0}$ to each of these subspaces is just a single Jordan block. The block in $W^{\prime \prime}$ is of type $\Delta_{m}^{\varepsilon}(0)$. The other two subspaces, $W$ and $W^{\prime}$, are totally isotropic. This implies that the restriction of $x_{0}$ to $W+W^{\prime}$ belongs to the type $\Delta_{n}^{+}(0)+\Delta_{n}^{-}(0)$. Hence $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$. Now let $t 
eq 0$. If $m=1$ one can easily check that $x(t)$ consists of two Jordan blocks of size $n+2$ and so $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$. Now let $m \geqslant 2$. Let $V_{1}$ be the $x(t)$-invariant subspace generated by $e_{0}^{\prime}$. A basis of $V_{1}$ consists of the vectors $e_{r}^{\prime}(0 \leqslant r \leqslant n)$ and $e_{m}^{\prime \prime}$. Let $V_{2}$ be the $x(t)$-invariant subspace generated by $e_{0}^{\prime \prime}$. A basis of $V_{2}$ consists of the vectors $e_{0}^{\prime \prime}, e_{r}^{\prime \prime}+t e_{r-1}\left(1 \leqslant r \leqslant m^{\prime}ight),(-1)^{r-m^{\prime}} e_{r}^{\prime \prime}+t e_{r-1}\left(m^{\prime}<r \leqslant might), \quad e_{r}$ $(m \leqslant r \leqslant n)$. We have $V_{1} \cap V_{2}=0$ and $\operatorname{dim} V_{1}=\operatorname{dim} V_{2}=n+2$. Since $x(t)^{n+2}=0$ and $$ x(t)^{m-2} e_{1}^{\prime \prime}=(-1)^{m-m^{\prime}-1} e_{m}^{\prime} 
otin V_{1}+V_{2}, \quad x(t)^{m-1} e_{1}^{\prime \prime} \in V_{1}, $$ it follows that $x(t)$ consists of three Jordan blocks whose sizes are $n+2, n+2$, and $m-1$. Since $\varepsilon(-1)^{m-m^{\prime}-1} f\left(e_{1}^{\prime \prime}, x(t)^{m-2} e_{1}^{\prime \prime}ight)=1$, it follows that the Jordan block of size $m-1$ belongs to the type $\Delta_{m-2}^{\varepsilon}(0)$. Hence $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ for $t 
eq 0$. Next assume that (9.1) has the form  egin{equation*} g^{+}(m+1)+g^{-}(m+1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+1) ightarrow 2 g(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+3), \quad m \leqslant n . 	ag{12.7} \end{equation*} We can choose a basis $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{m}, e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{m}^{\prime}, e_{0}^{\prime \prime}, \ldots, e_{n}^{\prime \prime}$ of $V$ such that $f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}ight)=f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0, f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime \prime}ight)=f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime \prime}ight)=0, f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=\delta_{r+s, m^{\prime}}$ for all $r, s$ and $f\left(e_{r}^{\prime \prime}, e_{s}^{\prime \prime}ight)=\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, n}$ for $r \leqslant s$. We define the family $x(t)$ by $$  egin{aligned} & x(t) e_{0}=e_{1}-\varepsilon t e_{0}^{\prime \prime} \quad\left(e_{1}=0 	ext { if } m=0ight), \ & x(t) e_{r}=e_{r+1} \quad(0<r<m), \ & x(t) e_{m}=0 \quad 	ext { if } m>0, \ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime}=-e_{r+1}^{\prime} \quad(0 \leqslant r<m), \quad x(t) e_{m}^{\prime}=0, \ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime \prime}=e_{r+1}^{\prime \prime} \quad\left(0 \leqslant r<n^{\prime}ight), \ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime \prime}=-e_{r+1}^{\prime \prime} \quad\left(n^{\prime} \leqslant r<night), \quad x(t) e_{n}^{\prime \prime}=t e_{m}^{\prime} . \end{aligned} $$ One can check that $x(t) \in L$ for all real $t$. As in the case (12.6) one can show that $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$. Now let $t 
eq 0$. An easy computation gives  egin{align*} & x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}=(-1)^{n-n^{\prime+1}} \varepsilon t^{2} e_{m}, \quad 	ext { and } \ & \varepsilon(-1)^{n-n^{\prime}+1} f\left(e_{0}, x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}ight)=t^{2} . 	ag{12.8} \end{align*} If $m=0$ then (12.8) implies that $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$. Now let $m \geqslant 1$. Then it is easy to verify that $x(t)$ consists of three Jordan blocks whose sizes are $n+3, m$, and $m$. The\ largest block corresponds to the $x(t)$-invariant subspace generated by $e_{0}$. It follows from (12.8) that this block belongs to the type $\Delta_{m+2}^{\varepsilon}(0)$, and so $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ for $t 
eq 0$. Next assume that the mutation (9.1) has the form  egin{align*} g^{+}(m+1)+g^{-}(m+1)+g^{+}(n+1)+g^{-}(n+1) &\ ightarrow 2 g(m)+2 g(n+2), \quad m \leqslant n . & 	ag{12.9}\end{align*} We can choose a basis $a_{0}, \ldots, a_{m}, a_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, a_{m}^{\prime}, b_{0}, \ldots, b_{n}, b_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, b_{n}^{\prime}$ of $V$ such that $f\left(a_{r}, a_{s}ight)=f\left(a_{r}^{\prime}, a_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0, f\left(b_{r}, b_{s}ight)=f\left(b_{r}^{\prime}, b_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0, f\left(a_{r}, b_{s}ight)=f\left(a_{r}^{\prime}, b_{s}ight)=f\left(a_{r}, b_{s}^{\prime}ight)$ $=f\left(a_{r}^{\prime}, b_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0, f\left(a_{r}, a_{s}^{\prime}ight)=\delta_{r+s, m}$, and $f\left(b_{r}, b_{s}^{\prime}ight)=\delta_{r+s, n}$ for all $r, s$. We define the family $x(t)$ of operators in $V$ by $$  egin{aligned} & x(t) a_{0}=a_{1}+t b_{0} \quad\left(a_{1}=0 	ext { if } m=0ight), \ & x(t) a_{r}=a_{r+1} \quad(0<r<m), \ & x(t) a_{m}=0 \quad 	ext { if } m>0, \ & x(t) a_{r}^{\prime}=-a_{r+1}^{\prime} \quad(0 \leqslant r<m), \quad x(t) a_{m}^{\prime}=0, \ & x(t) b_{r}=b_{r+1} \quad(0 \leqslant r<n), \quad x(t) b_{n}=0, \ & x(t) b_{r}^{\prime}=-b_{r+1}^{\prime} \quad(0 \leqslant r<n), \quad x(t) b_{n}^{\prime}=-t a_{m}^{\prime} . \end{aligned} $$ One can check that $x(t) \in L$ for all real $t$. By using the same argument as in the case (12.6) one can show that $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$. Now let $t 
eq 0$. Let $V_{1}$, resp. $V_{2}$, be the $x(t)$-invariant subspace generated by the vector $a_{0}$, resp. $b_{0}^{\prime}$. We have $$ x(t)^{n+1} b_{0}^{\prime}=(-1)^{n} x(t) b_{n}^{\prime}=(-1)^{n+1} t a_{m}^{\prime}, \quad x(t)^{n+2} b_{0}^{\prime}=0 . $$ For $m>0$ we have $x(t)^{n+1} a_{0}=x(t)^{n}\left(a_{1}+t b_{0}ight)=t x(t)^{n} b_{0}=t b_{n}$, and, for $m=0$, $x(t)^{n+1} a_{0}=t x(t)^{n} b_{0}=t b_{n}$. Thus for all $m$ we have $x(t)^{n+1} a_{0}=t b_{n}$ and $x(t)^{n+2} a_{0}=0$. It follows that $V_{1} \cap V_{2}=0$. If $m=0$ then $V=V_{1} \oplus V_{2}$, and so $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$. Now let $m \geqslant 1$. Then $x(t)^{n+2}=0$ and $\operatorname{dim} \operatorname{Ker} x(t)=4$. Thus $x(t)$ consists of four Jordan blocks; the two largest of them arise from $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$ and have size $n+2$. Since $x(t)^{m} V \subset V_{1}+V_{2}$, the other two Jordan blocks must be of size $m$ each. Therefore $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ for $t 
eq 0$. Next assume that the mutation (9.1) is of the form  egin{equation*} g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{-\varepsilon}(n+1) ightarrow g^{-\varepsilon}(m-1)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+3), \quad m \leqslant n . 	ag{12.10} \end{equation*} We can choose a basis $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{m+k}, e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{m+k}^{\prime}\left(k=n^{\prime}-m^{\prime}ight)$ of $V$ such that $f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}ight)=f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0$ and $f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=\varepsilon(-1)^{n-m^{\prime}+1} \delta_{r+s, m+k}$ for all $r, s$. We define the family $x(t)$ of operators in $V$ by $$  egin{aligned} & x(t) e_{r}=e_{r+1} \quad 	ext { for } r 
eq k-1, k+1, k+m, \ & x(t) e_{k-1}=e_{k}+(-1)^{m} e_{0}^{\prime} \quad 	ext { if } k>0, \ & x(t) e_{k+1}=e_{k+2}+(-1)^{m} t e_{0}^{\prime} \quad\left(e_{k+2}=0 	ext { if } m=1ight), \ & x(t) e_{k+m}=-t e_{m-1}^{\prime}-e_{m+1}^{\prime} \quad\left(e_{m+1}^{\prime}=0 	ext { if } k=0ight), \ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime}=-e_{r+1}^{\prime} \quad(0 \leqslant r<k+m), \quad x(t) e_{k+m}^{\prime}=0 . \end{aligned} $$ One can check that $x(t) \in L$ for all real $t$. If $k=0$ then $x_{0}$ consists of two Jordan blocks of size $m+1$. Since the subspaces spanned by $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{m+k}$ and $e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{m+k}^{\prime}$\ are $x_{0}$-invariant and totally isotropic, we have $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$. Now let $k \geqslant 1$. We have $$  egin{aligned} & x_{0}^{n} e_{0}=2(-1)^{k} e_{k+m}^{\prime}, \quad x_{0}^{m}\left((-1)^{m} e_{0}^{\prime}-e_{k}ight)=e_{m}^{\prime}-e_{k+m}, \ & x_{0}^{n+1} e_{0}=0, \quad x_{0}^{m+1}\left((-1)^{m} e_{0}^{\prime}-e_{k}ight)=0 . \end{aligned} $$ Hence $x_{0}$ consists of two Jordan blocks whose sizes are $n+1$ and $m+1$. Since $$ -\varepsilon(-1)^{n-n^{\prime}} f\left(e_{0}, x_{0}^{n} e_{0}ight)=2, \quad \varepsilon(-1)^{m-m^{\prime}} f\left((-1)^{m} e_{0}^{\prime}-e_{k}, e_{m}^{\prime}-e_{k+m}ight)=2, $$ we conclude that again $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$.\ Now let $t>0$. A simple computation gives $$ x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}=  egin{cases}2(-1)^{k} t e_{k+m}^{\prime} & 	ext { if } m>1, \ (-1)^{k} t e_{k+m}^{\prime} & 	ext { if } m=1,\end{cases} $$ and so  egin{equation*} \varepsilon(-1)^{n-n^{\prime}+1} f\left(e_{0}, x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}ight)>0 . 	ag{12.11} \end{equation*} Thus if $m=1$ then $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ for $t>0$. Now let $m \geqslant 2$. Then $x(t)$ consists of two Jordan blocks of sizes $n+3$ and $m-1$. It follows from (12.11) that the larger block belongs to the type $\Delta_{n+2}^{\varepsilon}(0)$. The same argument as in (12.2) implies that the other block belongs to the type $\Delta_{m-2}^{-\varepsilon}(0)$. Therefore $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ for $t>0$. Next assume that the mutation (9.1) is of the form  egin{equation*} 2 g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{-\varepsilon}(n+1) ightarrow 2 g(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+3), \quad m<n . 	ag{12.12} \end{equation*} We can choose a basis $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{m+k}, e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{m+k}^{\prime}, e_{0}^{\prime \prime}, \ldots, e_{m}^{\prime \prime}\left(k=n^{\prime}-m^{\prime}ight)$ of $V$ such that $f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}ight)=f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0, f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime \prime}ight)=f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime \prime}ight)=0, f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, k+m}$ for all $r, s$ and $f\left(e_{r}^{\prime \prime}, e_{s}^{\prime \prime}ight)=\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m}$ for $r \leqslant s$. The family of operators $x(t)$ in $V$ is defined by $$  egin{aligned} & x(t) e_{r}=e_{r+1} \quad 	ext { for } r 
eq k-1, k+m-m^{\prime}, k+m, \ & x(t) e_{k-1}=e_{k}-(-1)^{m^{\prime}} e_{0}^{\prime}, \ & x(t) e_{k+m-m^{\prime}}=e_{k+m-m^{\prime}+1}+t e_{m-m^{\prime}}^{\prime \prime} \quad 	ext { if } m>0, \ & x(t) e_{k+m}=(-1)^{m+m^{\prime}} e_{m+1}^{\prime} \quad 	ext { if } m>0, \ & x(t) e_{k}=(-1)^{m+m^{\prime}} e_{m+1}^{\prime}+t e_{m-m^{\prime}}^{\prime \prime} \quad 	ext { if } m=0, \ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime}=-e_{r+1}^{\prime} \quad(0 \leqslant r<k+m), \quad x(t) e_{k+m}^{\prime}=0, \ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime \prime}=e_{r+1}^{\prime \prime} \quad\left(0 \leqslant r<m^{\prime}ight), \ & x(t) e_{m^{\prime}}^{\prime \prime}=-t e_{m^{\prime}}^{\prime}-e_{m^{\prime}+1}^{\prime \prime} \quad\left(e_{m^{\prime}+1}^{\prime \prime}=0 	ext { if } m=m^{\prime}ight), \ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime \prime}=-e_{r+1}^{\prime \prime} \quad\left(m^{\prime}<r<might), \quad x(t) e_{m}^{\prime \prime}=0 \quad 	ext { if } m>1 . \end{aligned} $$ One can check that $x(t) \in L$ for all real $t$. We have  egin{align*} & x_{0}^{n} e_{0}=-2(-1)^{m+n^{\prime}} e_{k+m}^{\prime}, \quad x_{0} e_{k+m}^{\prime}=0, \ & -\varepsilon(-1)^{n-n^{\prime}} f\left(e_{0}, x_{0}^{n} e_{0}ight)=2 . 	ag{12.13} \end{align*} If $a=e_{k}+(-1)^{m^{\prime}} e_{0}^{\prime}$ and $b=e_{k+m}+(-1)^{m+m^{\prime}} e_{m}^{\prime}$ then we find that  egin{equation*} x_{0}^{m} a=b, \quad x_{0} b=0, \quad \varepsilon(-1)^{m-m^{\prime}} f\left(a, x_{0}^{m} aight)=2 . 	ag{12.14} \end{equation*} Note also that the restriction of $x_{0}$ to the subspace spanned by the vectors $e_{r}^{\prime \prime}$ is a Jordan block of type $\Delta_{m}^{\varepsilon}(0)$. Hence it follows from (12.13) and (12.14) that $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$. Now let $t 
eq 0$. An easy computation gives  egin{equation*} x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}=-(-1)^{k+m-m^{\prime}} t^{2} e_{k+m}^{\prime}, \quad \varepsilon(-1)^{n-n^{\prime}+1} f\left(e_{0}, x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}ight)=t^{2} . 	ag{12.15} \end{equation*} Thus if $m=0$ then $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$. Now let $m \geqslant 1$. Then $x(t)^{n+3}=0$ and $\operatorname{dim} \operatorname{Ker} x(t)=3$. Thus $x(t)$ consists of three Jordan blocks. By (12.15) the largest block is of size $n+3$ and belongs to the type $\Delta_{n+2}^{\varepsilon}(0)$. Let $W$ be the $x(t)$-invariant subspace generated by $e_{0}$. Then $\operatorname{dim} W=n+3$ and $x(t)^{m} V \subset W$. This implies that the remaining two Jordan blocks are of size $m$ each. Therefore $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ also when $m \geqslant 1$. Now assume that the mutation (9.1) is of the form  egin{equation*} g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+2 g^{-\varepsilon}(n+1) ightarrow g^{-\varepsilon}(m-1)+2 g(n+2), \quad m<n . 	ag{12.16} \end{equation*} We can choose a basis $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{m+k}, e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{m+k}^{\prime}, e_{0}^{\prime \prime}, \ldots, e_{n}^{\prime \prime}\left(k=n^{\prime}-m^{\prime}ight)$ of $V$ such that $f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}ight)=f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0, f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime \prime}ight)=f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime \prime}ight)=0, f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=-\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m+k}$ for all $r, s$ and $f\left(e_{r}^{\prime \prime}, e_{s}^{\prime \prime}ight)=-\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, n}$ for $r \leqslant s$. The family of operators $x(t)$ in $V$ is defined by $$  egin{aligned} & x(t) e_{0}=e_{1}+2 t e_{0}^{\prime \prime} \quad 	ext { if } k>1, \ & x(t) e_{0}=e_{1}-e_{0}^{\prime}+2 t e_{0}^{\prime \prime} \quad 	ext { if } k=1, \ & x(t) e_{r}=e_{r+1} \quad 	ext { for } r 
eq 0, k-1, k+1, k+m, \ & x(t) e_{k-1}=e_{k}+(-1)^{m^{\prime}} e_{0}^{\prime} \quad 	ext { if } k>1, \ & x(t) e_{k+1}=e_{k+2}+2 t^{2}(-1)^{m^{\prime}} e_{0}^{\prime} \quad 	ext { if } m>1, \ & x(t) e_{k+m}=-2 t^{2}(-1)^{m+m^{\prime}} e_{m-1}^{\prime}-(-1)^{m+m^{\prime}} e_{m+1}^{\prime} \quad 	ext { if } m>1, \ & x(t) e_{k+m}=-4 t^{2} e_{0}^{\prime}-e_{2}^{\prime} \quad 	ext { if } m=1, \ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime}=-e_{r+1}^{\prime} \quad(0 \leqslant r<k+m), \quad x(t) e_{k+m}^{\prime}=0, \ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime \prime}=e_{r+1}^{\prime \prime} \quad\left(0 \leqslant r<n^{\prime}ight), \ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime \prime}=-e_{r+1}^{\prime \prime} \quad\left(n^{\prime} \leqslant r<night), \quad x(t) e_{n}^{\prime \prime}=-2 t e_{k+m}^{\prime} . \end{aligned} $$ Note that $x(t)$ depends quadratically on $t$, i.e., $x(t)=x_{0}+x_{1} t+x_{2} t^{2}$ where $x_{0}, x_{1}, x_{2}$ are constant operators and $x_{2} 
eq 0$. One can check that $x(t) \in L$ for all real $t$. We have $x_{0}^{n} e_{0}=2(-1)^{m+n} e_{k+m}^{\prime}, x_{0}^{n+1} e_{0}=0$, and  egin{equation*} -\varepsilon(-1)^{n-n^{\prime}} f\left(e_{0}, x_{0}^{n} e_{0}ight)=2 . 	ag{12.17} \end{equation*} If $a=e_{k}-(-1)^{m^{\prime}} e_{0}^{\prime}$ and $b=e_{k+m}-(-1)^{m+m^{\prime}} e_{m}^{\prime}$ then $x_{0}^{m} a=b, x_{0} b=0$, and  egin{equation*} \varepsilon(-1)^{m-m^{\prime}} f\left(a, x_{0}^{m} aight)=2 . 	ag{12.18} \end{equation*} Note also that the restriction of $x_{0}$ to the subspace spanned by the vectors $e_{r}^{\prime \prime}$ is a Jordan block of type $\Delta_{n}^{-\varepsilon}(0)$. Hence it follows from (12.17) and (12.18) that $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$. Now let $t 
eq 0$. We have $$ x(t)^{n+2}=0 \quad 	ext { and } \quad x(t)^{n+1} e_{0}=2 t(-1)^{m+n^{\prime}}\left(-2 t e_{m+k-1}^{\prime}+e_{n}^{\prime \prime}ight) . $$ Hence $x(t)$ has a Jordan block of size $n+2$. But we know that such blocks must occur in pairs, and so there are two blocks of size $n+2$. Thus if $m=1$ then $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$. Now let $m \geqslant 2$. Since $\operatorname{dim} \operatorname{Ker} x(t)=3, x(t)$ consists of three Jordan blocks. Hence the remaining Jordan block has size $m-1$. By invoking the necessity part of Theorem 5 we can conclude that this block must be of type $\Delta_{m-2}^{-\varepsilon}(0)$. Therefore $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$. Finally, assume that the mutation (9.1) has the form  egin{equation*} 2 g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+2 g^{-\varepsilon}(n+1) ightarrow 2 g(m)+2 g(n+2), \quad m \leqslant n . 	ag{12.19} \end{equation*} Let $V=V_{1} \oplus V_{2}$ be an orthogonal decomposition with $V_{1}=W_{1} \oplus W_{1}^{\prime}$, $V_{2}=W_{2} \oplus W_{2}^{\prime}$ where $W_{1}, W_{1}^{\prime}, W_{2}, W_{2}^{\prime}$ are totally isotropic subspaces of dimension $m+k+1$ each $\left(k=n^{\prime}-m^{\prime}ight)$. We can choose bases $a_{0}, \ldots, a_{m+k} ; a_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, a_{m+k}^{\prime}$; $b_{0}, \ldots, b_{m+k}$; and $b_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, b_{m+k}^{\prime}$ of $W_{1}, W_{1}^{\prime}, W_{2}$, and $W_{2}^{\prime}$, respectively, such that $f\left(a_{r}, a_{s}^{\prime}ight)=f\left(b_{r}, b_{s}^{\prime}ight)=(-1)^{n-m^{\prime}+1} \varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m+k}$ for all $r, s$. Let $x_{0}$ be the operator in $V$ defined by $$  egin{aligned} & x_{0} a_{r}=a_{r+1} \quad 	ext { for } r 
eq k-1, k+m, \ & x^{0} a_{k-1}=a_{k}+(-1)^{m} a_{0}^{\prime} \quad 	ext { if } k>0, \ & x_{0} a_{k+m}=-a_{m+1}^{\prime} \quad\left(a_{m+1}^{\prime}=0 	ext { if } k=0ight), \ & x_{0} a_{r}^{\prime}=-a_{r+1}^{\prime} \quad(0 \leqslant r<m+k), \quad x_{0} a_{m+k}^{\prime}=0, \end{aligned} $$ and by analogous formulas obtained from these by replacing $a$ with $b$ everywhere. From the case (12.10) it follows that $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$. We make $V$ into a complex vector space by defining the action of $i$ by $i a_{r}=b_{r}$ and $i a_{r}^{\prime}=b_{r}^{\prime}$ for all $r$. We shall denote $V$ with this complex structure by $V^{\prime}$. Note that $a_{0}, \ldots, a_{m+k}, a_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, a_{m+k}^{\prime}$ is a basis of $V^{\prime}$. There exists a unique hermitian form $f^{\prime}$ on $V^{\prime}$ such that $\operatorname{Re} f^{\prime}=f$ for $j=6$ (then $f$ is symmetric) and $\operatorname{Im} f^{\prime}=f$ for $j=9$ (then $f$ is skew-symmetric). Indeed $f^{\prime}$ is determined by $$  egin{array}{ll} f^{\prime}\left(a_{r}, a_{s}ight)=f^{\prime}\left(a_{r}^{\prime}, a_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0, & \ f^{\prime}\left(a_{r}, a_{s}^{\prime}ight)=(-1)^{n-m^{\prime}+1} \varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m+k} & 	ext { if } j=6, \ f^{\prime}\left(a_{r}, a_{s}^{\prime}ight)=(-1)^{n-m^{\prime+1}} i \varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m+k} & 	ext { if } j=9 . \end{array} $$ It is clear that $f^{\prime}$ is nondegenerate and $\operatorname{sig}\left(f^{\prime}ight)=(k+m, k+m)$. Let $U$ be the classical group of the fourth series defined by the pair $\left(V^{\prime}, f^{\prime}ight)$. Clearly $U$ is a subgroup of $G$ and we shall view its Lie algebra $M$ as a subalgebra of $L$. Note that $x_{0}$ is a complex linear operator in $V^{\prime}$ and that $x_{0} \in M$. Let $Y_{1}=g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{-\varepsilon}(n+1)$ and $Y_{2}=g^{-\varepsilon}(m)+g^{\varepsilon}(n+2)$. Note that $\operatorname{sig} Y_{1}=\operatorname{sig} Y_{2}=(k+m, k+m)$. Let $\mathcal{O}_{r}^{\prime}(r=1,2)$ be the nilpotent orbit of $U$ in $M$ corresponding to the chromosome $Y_{r}$. Note that $x_{0}$ as a complex linear operator consists of two Jordan blocks whose sizes are $n+1$ and $m+1$. We claim that $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime}$. If $n=m$ this follows from the fact that $x_{0}$ has a totally isotropic Jordan block, for instance, its restriction to the subspace of $V^{\prime}$ spanned by the vectors $a_{r}$. Now let $k>0$. Then by using $x_{0}^{n} a_{0}=2(-1)^{k} a_{m+k}^{\prime}$ and (12.1) we find that $(-i)^{n}(-\varepsilon) f^{\prime}\left(a_{0}, x_{0}^{n} a_{0}ight)=2$, and so by (5.3) the larger block of $x_{0}$ is of type $\Delta_{n}^{-\varepsilon}(0)$. Similarly one can check that the other block is of type $\Delta_{m}^{\varepsilon}(0)$, and consequently\ $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime}$. This implies that $\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime} \subset \mathcal{O}_{1}$. On the other hand it is clear that $\mathcal{O}_{2}^{\prime} \subset \mathcal{O}_{2}$. Since $Y_{1} \leqslant Y_{2}$, we have $\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime} \leqslant \mathcal{O}_{2}^{\prime}$ by the case $j=4$ of Theorem 5. Consequently $\mathcal{O}_{1} \leqslant \mathcal{O}_{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Section 12: the cases j=6,9

nodes.name: Notation m' and sign identity (12.1)
nodes.statement: 12. The cases $j=6,9$. These two cases will be treated simultaneously. Recall that $\Phi_{6}=(2 \Lambda, \Pi)$ and $\Phi_{9}=(\Pi, 2 \Lambda)$. If $m(\geqslant 0)$ is an integer we shall write $m^{\prime}=\left[\frac{1}{2}(m+1)\right]$. Thus $m=2 m^{\prime}$ for $m$ even and $m=2 m^{\prime}-1$ for $m$ odd. We have \begin{equation*} (-1)^{m-m^{\prime}}= \begin{cases}i^{m} & \text { if } m \text { is even, } \\ i^{m-1} & \text { if } m \text { is odd. }\end{cases} \tag{12.1} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Notation m' and sign identity (12.1)

nodes.name: Mutation (12.2): family, Jordan blocks, ad hoc argument via
nodes.statement: Assume first that the mutation (9.1) has the form \begin{equation*} 2 g(m+1) \rightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m)+g^{-\varepsilon}(m+2) \text {. } \tag{12.2} \end{equation*} We can choose a basis $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{m}, e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{m}^{\prime}$ of $V$ such that $f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}\right)=f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}\right)=0$ and $f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}\right)=\delta_{r+s, m}$ for all $r, s$. We define the one-parameter family $x(t)=x_{0}+t x_{1}$ of operators in $V$ by $$ \begin{aligned} & x(t) e_{0}=e_{1}-\varepsilon(-1)^{m+m^{\prime}} t e_{0}^{\prime} \quad \text { if } m>0 \\ & x(t) e_{r}=e_{r+1} \quad(0<r<m), \quad x(t) e_{m}=-\varepsilon(-1)^{m^{\prime}} t e_{m}^{\prime}, \\ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime}=-e_{r+1}^{\prime} \quad(0 \leqslant r<m), \quad x(t) e_{m}^{\prime}=0 . \end{aligned} $$ It is easy to verify that $x(t) \in L$ for all real $t$. Since $x_{0}$ consists of two Jordan blocks of size $m+1$ each, we have $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$. (Note that $m$ is odd if $j=6$ and $m$ is even if $j=9$.) We have \begin{equation*} x(t)^{m+1} e_{0}=-2 \varepsilon(-1)^{m^{\prime}} t e_{m}^{\prime} \quad \text { and } \quad-\varepsilon i^{2 m^{\prime}} f\left(e_{0}, x(t)^{m+1} e_{0}\right)=2 t . \tag{12.3} \end{equation*} Now let $t>0$. If $m=0$ then $x(t)$ is a single Jordan block and by (5.4)-(5.5) we have $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$. Now let $m \geqslant 1$. Then $x(t)^{m+2}=0$ and $\operatorname{dim} \operatorname{Ker} x(t)=2$. It follows that $x(t)$ consists of two Jordan blocks whose sizes are $m+2$ and $m$. The larger block is the type $\Delta_{m+1}^{-\varepsilon}(0)$ because of (12.3). To avoid tedious computations which are needed to determine the type of the smaller block, we shall use the following ad\\ hoc argument. The smaller block is either of type $\Delta_{m-1}^{\varepsilon}(0)$ or of type $\Delta_{m-1}^{-\varepsilon}(0)$. When we let $t \rightarrow 0(t>0)$ the type must become $\Delta_{m-1}^{\varepsilon}(0)$. Otherwise there is a strictly decreasing sequence $t_{1}, t_{2}, \ldots$ with limit 0 for which the smaller block is of type $\Delta_{m-1}^{-\varepsilon}(0)$. By the necessity part of Theorem 5, we then obtain $2 g(m+1) \leqslant$ $g^{-\varepsilon}(m+2)+g^{-\varepsilon}(m)$. By applying the priming operation $m-1$ times (see §6) we obtain $2 g(2) \leqslant g^{-\varepsilon}(3)+g^{-\varepsilon}(1)$, which is false. Hence for small positive $t$ the smaller block is of type $\Delta_{m-1}^{\varepsilon}(0)$. Consequently for small positive $t$ we have $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$. Since the set of all $t$ for which the smaller block is of type $\Delta_{m-1}^{\varepsilon}(0)$ (or $\Delta_{m-1}^{-\varepsilon}(0)$ ) is open, it follows that in fact $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ for all $t>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Mutation (12.2): family, Jordan blocks, ad hoc argument via necessity of Theorem 5

nodes.name: Mutation (12.4)
nodes.statement: Next assume that (9.1) has the form \begin{equation*} g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(n+1) \rightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m-1)+g^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(n+3), \quad m \leqslant n . \tag{12.4} \end{equation*} We can choose a basis $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{m}, e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{n}^{\prime}$ of $V$ such that $f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}\right)=0$ for all $r, s$ and $f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}\right)=\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m}$ and $f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}\right)=\varepsilon^{\prime} \delta_{r+s, n}$ for $r \leqslant s$. The family $x(t)$ is defined by $$ \begin{aligned} & x(t) e_{0}=e_{1}+\varepsilon t e_{0}^{\prime}, \\ & x(t) e_{r}=e_{r+1} \quad\left(0<r<m^{\prime}\right), \\ & x(t) e_{r}=-e_{r+1} \quad\left(m^{\prime} \leqslant r<m\right), \\ & x(t) e_{m}=0, \\ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime}=e_{r+1}^{\prime} \quad\left(0 \leqslant r<n^{\prime}\right), \\ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime}=-e_{r+1}^{\prime} \quad\left(n^{\prime} \leqslant r<n\right), \\ & x(t) e_{n}^{\prime}=-\varepsilon^{\prime} t e_{m} . \end{aligned} $$ One can easily verify that $x_{0}$ and $x_{1}$ are in $L$ and so $x(t) \in L$ for all real $t$. Moreover it is clear that $x_{0} \in \mathcal{O}_{1}$ (see §5). We have \begin{align*} & x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}=-\varepsilon \varepsilon^{\prime}(-1)^{n-n^{\prime}} t^{2} e_{m}, \quad \text { and } \\ & \varepsilon^{\prime}(-1)^{n-n^{\prime}+1} f\left(e_{0}, x(t)^{n+2} e_{0}\right)=t^{2} . \tag{12.5} \end{align*} Now let $t>0$. If $m=1$ then $x(t)$ is a single Jordan block and (12.5) and (5.4)-(5.5) show that it is of type $\Delta_{n+2}^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(0)$. Thus $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ in this case. Now let $m \geqslant 2$. Since $x(t)^{n+3}=0$ and $\operatorname{dim} \operatorname{Ker} x(t)=2, x(t)$ consists of two Jordan blocks whose sizes are $n+3$ and $m-1$. The larger block is of type $\Delta_{n+2}^{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(0)$, by (12.5) and (5.4)-(5.5). As in the case (12.2) we can conclude that for $t>0$ the other Jordan block of $x(t)$ must belong to the type $\Delta_{m-2}^{\varepsilon}(0)$. Thus $x(t) \in \mathcal{O}_{2}$ for $t>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Mutation (12.4)

nodes.name: Mutation (12.6)
nodes.statement:
Now assume that the mutation (9.1) has the form  egin{align*} g^{\varepsilon}(m+1)+g^{+}(n & +1)+g^{-}(n+1) \ & ightarrow g^{\varepsilon}(m-1)+2 g(n+2), \quad m \leqslant n . 	ag{12.6} \end{align*} We can choose a basis $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{n}, e_{0}^{\prime}, \ldots, e_{n}^{\prime}, e_{0}^{\prime \prime}, \ldots, e_{m}^{\prime \prime}$ of $V$ such that $f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}ight)=f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=0, f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime \prime}ight)=f\left(e_{r}^{\prime}, e_{s}^{\prime \prime}ight)=0, f\left(e_{r}, e_{s}^{\prime}ight)=\delta_{r+s, n}$ for all $r, s$ and $f\left(e_{r}^{\prime \prime}, e_{s}^{\prime \prime}ight)=\varepsilon \delta_{r+s, m}$ for $r \leqslant s$. The family $x(t)$ of operators in $V$ is defined by $$  egin{aligned} & x(t) e_{r}=e_{r+1} \quad(0 \leqslant r<n), \quad x(t) e_{n}=0 \ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime}=-e_{r+1}^{\prime} \quad(0 \leqslant r<n), \quad x(t) e_{n}^{\prime}=-\varepsilon t e_{m}^{\prime \prime}, \end{aligned} $$ $$  egin{aligned} & x(t) e_{0}^{\prime \prime}=e_{1}^{\prime \prime}+t e_{0}, \ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime \prime}=e_{r+1}^{\prime \prime} \quad\left(0<r<m^{\prime}ight), \ & x(t) e_{r}^{\prime \prime}=-e_{r+1}^{\prime \prime} \quad\left(m^{\prime} \leqslant r<might), \quad x(t) e_{m}^{\prime \prime}=0 . \end{aligned} $$ One can check that $x(t) \in L$ for all real $t$. Let $W, W^{\prime}$ and $W^{\prime \prime}$ be the subspaces of $V$ spanned by the vectors $e_{r}, e_{r}^{\prime}$ and $e_{r}^{\prime \prime}$, respectively. These subspaces are invariant under $x_{0}=x(0)$ and $W^{\prime \prime} \perp\left(W+W^{\prime}ight)$. The restriction of $x_{0}$ to each of these subspaces is just a single Jordan block.
